A pressure delivery device (PDD) is made using improvised materials, such as a shoe or boot, full water bottle, or canteen which applies additional pressure to the wound after it has been packed. A PDD may be needed to apply additional and targeted pressure to control inguinal or groin hemorrhage.

For groin injuries packed with hemostatic dressings, use an improvised junctional PDD to secure the dressing. The PDD is placed in the groin while continuously maintaining pressure to the dressing. 57

The PDD is then secured with a TQ, which is wrapped over the hips with the windlass or ratchet placed directly over the improvised device and tightened to add additional pressure. Two TQs placed together may be needed when improvising a PDD. Note. Junctional hemorrhages involve larger blood vessels requiring more pressure (and targeted pressure) than can be applied with a pressure dressing alone.

Inguinal (Groin) Hemorrhage Control with Improvised Junctional Pressure Device: • Consider body substance isolation. • Expose the injury and assess the bleeding source. • Apply direct pressure to the wound using a hand, fist, or elbow and open the hemostatic gauze package. • Tightly pack the wound with hemostatic gauze until the wound cavity is filled (finishing the packing within 90 seconds). • Hold pressure for a minimum of 3 minutes. • Reassess to ensure that the bleeding has been controlled while maintaining pressure. • If packed with hemostatic dressing, and extra hemostatic dressings are available, remove and repack. • If packed with gauze or initially packed with hemostatic dressing and no more hemostatic dressing is available, apply additional gauze and pressure (for three minutes) until bleeding stops. • Select and position a pressure delivery device, such as a canteen, into the inguinal gutter while maintaining pressure. • Select a TQ that can wrap around the casualty's waist/hip area or connect the two tourniquets together. • Place the windlass or ratchet TQ directly over the middle of the pressure delivery device; ensure that the routing buckle is located towards the middle of the body. • Remove all slack from the band or strap using a pushing motion across the casualty's body before tightening the TQ. • Tighten the TQ and ensure that the bleeding is still controlled, and the distal pulse is absent. Note. If the bleeding is not controlled and the distal pulse (a pulse located below the TQ) is present, remove any remaining slack in the strapping (if possible) and

After massive bleeding is controlled, the responder can move on to airway control, the first "A" in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. The casualty must have an open (unobstructed) airway. If the casualty is awake and talking, you can assume the casualty's airway is open. However, the casualty may still have difficulty breathing. If the casualty is unconscious, their airway must be inspected for any obvious blockages.

Humans must have oxygen to live. Through the breathing process, the lungs draw oxygen from the air and put it into the blood. The heart pumps the blood through the body to be used by the cells that require a constant supply of oxygen. Some cells are more dependent on a constant supply of oxygen than others. For example, cells of the brain may die within five minutes without oxygen. The brain, heart and lungs are very intolerant to lack of oxygen. The brain is considered one of the organs that is least tolerant to oxygen deprivation. Once these cells die, they are lost forever and do not regenerate. This could result in permanent brain damage, paralysis, or death.

Airway obstruction on the battlefield is often due to facial trauma. If the casualty is breathing on their own but unconscious or semi-conscious, and there is no airway obstruction, further airway management is achieved through a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA). First responders must assess casualties with facial trauma when contraindications exist to NPA use (such as basilar skull fractures, disruption of the midface, nasopharynx, or roof of the mouth).

Unconscious casualties can also lose their airway as the muscles of their tongue may have relaxed. This causes the tongue to block the airway by sliding to the back of the mouth and covering the opening to the windpipe. The signs and symptoms of airway obstruction include: • Casualty is in distress and indicating that they cannot breathe properly. • Casualty making snoring or gurgling sounds. • Visible blood or foreign objects are present in the airway. • Severe trauma to the face is observed.

Respiration is the process where we breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. The efficiency of this process can vary depending on someone's age and physical health. Generally, adults breathe 12 to 20 times a minute. But children and infants have different rates. For instance, children aged one to 10 years take 15 to 30 breaths per minute. Infants who are six to 12 months old breath faster, at a rate of 25 to 50 times per minute. Meanwhile, the youngest infants, those aged zero to five months, have a rate of 25 to 40 breaths per minute.

sections.section: Anatomy and physiology of the respiratory system
sections.text: The respiratory system consists of the airway, lungs, and rib cage. The airway consists of the nose, mouth, throat, voice box, and windpipe. Air passes to and from the lungs through the canal. The lungs are two elastic organs made up of thousands of tiny air spaces or sacs and covered by an airtight membrane. The bronchial tree is a part of the lungs. The rib cage is the structure that joins the spine in the back and the breastbone in front, which protects the heart and lungs. The top part of the rib cage is closed by the structure of the neck, and the bottom part is separated from the abdominal cavity by a large dome-shaped muscle called the diaphragm (figure 5-1 on page 60). 59

sections.section: Anatomy and physiology of the respiratory system
sections.text: The diaphragm and rib muscles, which are under the control of the respiratory center in the brain, automatically contract and relax. Inspiration increases and expiration decreases the size of the rib cage. When the rib cage increases and then decreases, the air pressure in the lungs is first less and then more than the atmospheric pressure, thus causing the air to rush into and out of the lungs to equalize the pressure.

The CoTCCC-recommended NPA with lubricant is a nonsterile, rubber tube-shaped device that is inserted into the nostril of a casualty. It acts as a wedge to keep the airway open by keeping the tongue from falling back into the space behind the mouth leading to the windpipe. Only an NPA, size 32 French, is found within the standard issued JFAKs. Sizing the NPA before insertion is not necessary but is important to minimize nasopharyngeal trauma or elicit the casualty's gag reflex. The lubricant is a water-based substance that assists in inserting the device into the nose. Use of an NPA is a Tier 2 skill.

Tier 1 TCCC skills for airway control encompass techniques and procedures designed to address various challenges, including airway obstructions and respiratory distress. Proficiency in these skills is imperative for Service members operating in high-stakes, dynamic situations, and where swift and precise intervention can mean the difference between life, and death on the battlefield.

sections.section: Safely position the casualty to open the airway
sections.text: Check for responsiveness (figure 5-2 step A on page 61) and establish whether the casualty is conscious by gently shaking them and asking, "Are you OK?" Call for help (figure 5-2 step B on page 61) and then position the unconscious casualty so that they are lying in the recovery position, head tilted back; chin away from chest (figure 5-2 step C on page 61) by — • Straightening the casualty's legs. • Moving the casualty's arm that is nearest to you. Move it so that it is straight and above their head. Repeat the procedure for the other arm placing it by their side. • Kneeling beside the casualty with your knees near their shoulders (leave space to roll their body). • Placing one hand behind their head and neck for support. On your other hand, grasp the casualty under their arm (figure 5-2 step C on page 61). • Rolling the casualty towards you using a steady, even pull. The casualty's head and neck should stay in line with their back. 60 Airway Control

sections.section: Safely position the casualty to open the airway
sections.text: The recovery position allows blood and mucus to drain out of the casualty's nose and mouth and not drain back into the airway. However, if a neck injury is suspected and the jaw-thrust technique will be used, kneel at the casualty's head, looking towards their feet.

Oxygen flows to and from the lungs requires an unobstructed airway, yet obstructions can arise due to various factors: 61 • • • • Unconsciousness may lead to the tongue falling back into the throat, obstructing the airway if not properly managed. Foreign objects, particularly food, may become lodged in the throat during eating, especially when large pieces are swallowed without proper chewing, exacerbated by factors like alcohol consumption or slipping dentures. Regurgitation of stomach contents or the formation of blood clots due to head and facial injuries can further contribute to airway blockage. Ensure correct positioning and maintenance of the airway in injured or unconscious casualties to mitigate these risks.

Upper airway obstruction, a potentially life-threatening emergency, can occur as either a partial or complete blockage. The severity and nature of the obstruction underscore the importance of rapid recognition and immediate intervention to prevent respiratory compromise. Identifying the signs early and responding effectively are crucial in maintaining the airway and supporting breathing, which are vital for the casualty's survival. This situation demands prompt and decisive action to alleviate the obstruction and ensure an open airway.

The casualty may still have an air exchange. A good air exchange means that the casualty can cough forcefully, though they may be wheezing between coughs. The rescuer should not interfere and should encourage the casualty to cough up the object obstructing their airway on their own. Weak coughing with a high-pitched noise between coughs may indicate a poor air exchange. You should assist the casualty and treat them as though they had a complete obstruction.

A complete obstruction (no air exchange) is indicated if the casualty cannot speak, breathe, or cough at all. They may be clutching their neck and moving erratically. In an unconscious casualty, a complete obstruction is also indicated if after opening their airway you cannot ventilate them. A casualty, experiencing a partial foreign body airway obstruction, with poor air exchange, or a complete airway obstruction will not survive without medical intervention. Both conditions are treated the same. OPENING THE AIRWAY OF AN UNCONSCIOUS OR NOT BREATHING CASUALTY 7B

The tongue is the single most common cause of an airway obstruction (see figure 5-3). In most cases, simply using the head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw thrust technique can open the airway. This action pulls the tongue away from the air passage in the throat (see figure 5-4).
Call for help and then position the casualty. Move (roll) the casualty onto their back as described in paragraph 5-10 on page 60. 62 Airway Control

If a foreign body is seen in the airway, an attempt to remove it should be made. Do not put your fingers in the mouth to try to find or remove any unseen objects that might be causing an obstruction as this may push the object further into the airway. Open the airway using the head-tilt/chin-lift method. Note. If foreign material or vomitus is visible in the mouth, it should be removed as quickly as possible.

Place one hand on the casualty's forehead and apply firm, backward pressure with the palm to tilt the head back. Place the fingertips of the other hand under the bony part of the lower jaw and lift, bringing the chin forward. The thumb should not be used to lift the chin (see figure 5-5). Note. The fingers should not press deeply into the soft tissue under the chin because the airway may be obstructed. 63 Jaw-Thrust Method 352B

The jaw-thrust method may be accomplished by the rescuer grasping the angles of the casualty's lower jaw and lifting with both hands, one on each side, displacing the jaw forward and up (see figure 5-6). The rescuer's elbows should rest on the surface on which the casualty is lying. If the lips close, the lower lip can be retracted with the thumb. If mouth-to-mouth breathing is necessary, close the nostrils by placing your cheek tightly against them. The head should be carefully supported without tilting it backwards or turning it from side-to-side. If this is unsuccessful, the head should be tilted back slightly. The jaw-thrust is the safest first approach to opening the airway of a casualty who has a suspected neck injury because in most cases it can be accomplished without extending the neck. Note. If the casualty's lips are still closed after the jaw has been moved forward, use your thumbs to retract the lower lip, and allow air to enter the casualty's mouth.

The jaw-thrust method, commonly emphasized in training, can sometimes serve as a distraction in the field. Neck injuries in trauma cases are typically associated with dramatic incidents such as falls and motor vehicle accidents. Most neck injuries occur upon impact, and the extent of injury is usually immediate and unchangeable at the scene. If neck trauma is present, it is often necessary to perform a jaw-thrust maneuver to secure an airway and maintain that position until additional personnel arrive. This intervention allows the responder to proceed with the MARCH sequence.

If the casualty is breathing independently yet is unconscious or semiconscious, and there is no airway obstruction, managing the airway is best accomplished using an NPA. An NPA is suitable for both conscious and unconscious individuals and is effective in helping to open or maintain an open airway. This method ensures that the airway remains clear, facilitating easier breathing and potentially preventing further complications.

Casualties with severe facial trauma can often protect their own airways by sitting up and leaning forward. Assisting a conscious casualty by helping them assume any comfortable sitting-up position that allows them to breathe easily. If the casualty is unconscious but breathing, the casualty should be placed in the recovery position (figure 5-7 on page 65). 64 Airway Control

The recovery position allows blood and mucus to drain out of the casualty's nose and mouth and not drain back into the airway. The recovery position also helps to protect against inhaling vomit if the casualty throws up. If a casualty can breathe on their own, let them assume the best position (position of comfort) that allows them to breathe, including sitting up.

The primary objective of Tier 2 airway control skills is to confirm the initiation of Tier 1 skills, with the addition of Tier 2 insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway and monitor the casualty for any signs of airway compromise, as outlined in paragraph 5-3. If the casualty shows signs of not breathing spontaneously, it's imperative to promptly notify medical personnel. Medical personnel may then require assistance from the CLS in administering breathing assistance using a bag valve mask (BVM) device, as depicted in figure 5-8. In instances where respirations are observed to be diminished, providing ventilation support with a BVM becomes necessary, and the CLS may be requested to assist in its usage by medical personnel.

Casualties requiring ongoing BVM support due to lack of spontaneous breathing effort, if not just administered a sedating pain medication, might indicate an injury or condition warranting earlier or immediate evacuation (such as severe traumatic brain injury or TBI). If definitive treatment or evacuation is not available, consider triaging the casualty to expectant if resources are limited or better applied to more likely survivable casualties.

Ventilations can be performed alone or with two people working together. The mask is held using the "E-C" holding technique (figure 5-9 on page 66). The mask is sealed over the casualty's mouth so that air does not escape (figure 5-10 on page 66). The mask is then squeezed firmly for one to two seconds and five to six seconds apart. The Deployed Medicine website has an instruction video on the proper application of the one and two-person BVM. 65 technique casualty

Expedient techniques for airway control are critically important in TCCC due to the immediate threat posed by compromised airways in combat situations. Injured Service members may experience airway obstructions, respiratory distress, or loss of consciousness, which can rapidly progress to life-threatening situations. Expedient airway control techniques, such as the head tilt/chin lift, jaw thrust maneuver and use of NPAs may enable prompt restoration of adequate breathing and oxygenation. These techniques can be quickly implemented by trained personnel, ensuring timely intervention even in chaotic and high-stress environments. By swiftly addressing airway compromises, through the use of expedient techniques in TCCC play a vital role in preserving life, preventing further complications, and maximizing the chances of survival for injured military personnel on the battlefield. OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY – CONSCIOUS CASUALTY 79B

Clearing an airway obstruction in a conscious casualty can be managed while they are either standing or sitting. However, it's critical to recognize that an obstructed airway can lead to oxygen deficiency in the brain, resulting in respiratory arrest, unconsciousness and, if not promptly corrected, death.

To assess and manage airway obstruction, start by asking the casualty if they can speak or if they are choking. Additionally, check for the universal choking sign (see figure 5-11 on page 67). If the casualty can speak or cough effectively, encourage them to continue coughing. This indicates that they still have good air exchange, and you should not interfere with their efforts to expel the obstruction. 66 Airway Control

However, if you notice high-pitched sounds when the casualty breathes or coughs, indicating poor air exchange, or if the casualty is unable to breathe, immediate action is required. Call for help and prepare to perform manual thrusts to clear the obstruction. Use abdominal thrusts, also known as the Heimlich maneuver, by positioning your hands between the waist and the rib cage and delivering quick upward thrusts. For individuals in advanced stages of pregnancy, those who are markedly obese, or if there is a significant abdominal wound, use chest thrust instead. This involves placing your hands in the center of the breastbone and pushing sharply inward and upward.

Quick action is essential in these situations to restore breathing and prevent further complications, including death. Always ensure to assess the situation carefully and apply the appropriate technique based on the casualty's condition Apply Abdominal Thrusts 35B

Prior to applying abdominal thrust, first responders should administer five back blows. Abdominal thrust can be accomplished by using the following procedures: • Stand behind the casualty and wrap your arms around their waist. • Make a fist with one hand and grasp it with the other. The thumb side of your fist should be against the casualty's abdomen, in the midline and slightly above the casualty's navel, but well below the tip of the breastbone (figure 5-12 on page 68). • Press the fists into the abdomen with a quick backward and upward thrust (figure 5-13 on page 68). 67 abdominal thrust procedure • • • abdominal thrust Each thrust should be a separate and distinct movement. Continue performing abdominal thrusts until the obstruction is expelled or the casualty becomes unresponsive. If the casualty becomes unresponsive, call for help as you proceed with the steps to open the airway.

An alternate technique to the abdominal thrust is the chest thrust. This technique is useful when the casualty has an abdominal wound, is pregnant, or when the casualty is so large that you cannot wrap your arms around the abdomen. To apply chest thrusts with casualty sitting or standing: • Stand behind the casualty and wrap your arms around their chest with your arms under their armpits. • Make a fist with one hand and place the thumb side of the fist in the middle of the breastbone (take care to avoid the tip of the breastbone and the margins of the ribs). • Grasp the fist with the other hand and exert thrusts (figure 5-14 on page 69). 68 Airway Control • • • Each thrust should be delivered slowly, distinctly, and with the intent of relieving the obstruction. Perform chest thrusts until the obstruction is expelled or the casualty becomes unresponsive. If the casualty becomes unresponsive, call for help as you proceed with steps to open the airway, and perform rescue breathing. OPENING THE OBSTRUCTED AIRWAY – CASUALTY LYING DOWN OR UNRESPONSIVE 80B

When an individual who is choking becomes unresponsive while lying down, or if an unconscious person is discovered and the cause of their condition is unknown, specific emergency protocols must be followed to address potential airway obstruction.

If a conscious individual begins choking and subsequently loses consciousness, immediate action is required: • Summon help right away to ensure assistance is on the way. • Open the casualty's airway to assess and manage the obstruction. • Perform a finger sweep only if there is visible obstruction in the mouth to avoid pushing the obstruction deeper. • Attempt to rescue breathing, which involves assessing whether the air can flow into the lungs. Refer to detailed instructions on mouth-to-mouth resuscitation provided in paragraph 6-49 on page 81. If breathing efforts fail due to a blockage, swiftly move to clear the airway using procedures outlined in paragraph 5-39.

In scenarios where a casualty is found already unresponsive, the procedure slightly differs: • Quickly assess the situation to understand the context and severity. • Call for immediate assistance. • Position the casualty on their back to manage and secure the airway effectively. • Check for a pulse to determine the urgency of cardiovascular support. • Open the airway using recommended techniques. • Confirm if the casualty is not breathing and, if so, proceed to attempt rescue breathing as per the guidelines detailed in paragraph 6-49 on page 81.

These critical steps are designed to maximize the chances of recovery by ensuring that the airway is cleared, and that breathing is restored at the earliest possible opportunity. Quick and effective intervention is crucial in such emergencies, underscoring the importance of thorough training and readiness. 69

If you are still unable to ventilate the casualty, perform 6 to 10 manual (abdominal or chest) thrusts. To perform the abdominal thrusts: • Kneel astride the casualty's thighs (see below figure 5-15). • • • • Place the heel of one hand against the casualty's abdomen (in the midline slightly above the navel but well below the tip of the breastbone). Place your other hand on top of the first one. Point your fingers toward the casualty's head. Press into the casualty's abdomen with a quick, forward, and upward thrust. You can use your body weight to perform the maneuver. Deliver each thrust quickly and distinctly. Repeat the sequence of abdominal thrusts, finger sweeping, and rescue breathing (attempt to ventilate) as long as necessary to remove the object from the obstructed airway. If the casualty's chest rises, proceed to feel for their pulse.

To perform chest thrusts the unresponsive casualty is placed on their back, face up, and open their mouth. The first responder kneels close to the side of the casualty's body and— • Locates the lower edge of the casualty's ribs with their fingers by running theirs fingers up along the rib cage to the notch (figure 5-16 step A on page 71). • Places the middle finger on the notch in the casualty's chest and the index finger next to the middle finger on the lower edge of the casualty's breastbone. • Place the heel of the other hand on the lower half of the breastbone next to the two fingers (figure 5-16 step B on page 71). • Remove the fingers from the notch and place that hand on top of the positioned hand on the breastbone, extending or interlocking the fingers (figure 5-16 step C on page 71). • Straighten and lock elbows with their shoulders directly above the hands without bending the elbows, rocking, or allowing the shoulders to sag. • Apply enough pressure to depress the breastbone 1½ to 2 inches and then release the pressure completely (figure 5-16 step D on page 71). This press and release process is delivered quickly and distinctly, six to 10 times. Figure 5-17 on page 71 shows another view of the breastbone being depressed.

The first responder repeats the sequence of the chest thrust, finger sweep, and rescue breathing as long as necessary to clear the object from the obstructed airway. If the casualty's chest rises, proceed to feeling for their pulse.

If rescue breathing cannot be administered due to airway obstruction, remove the airway obstruction by— • Placing the casualty on their back, face up, turn the unresponsive casualty as a unit, and call out for help. • Performing a finger sweep. 71 • Using the tongue-jaw lift by opening the casualty's mouth by grasping both their tongue and lower jaw between your thumb and fingers and lifting (tongue-jaw lift) (see figure 5-18). If you are unable to open their mouth, cross your fingers and thumb (crossed-finger method) and push their teeth apart (see figure 5-19) by pressing your thumb against their upper teeth and pressing your finger against their lower teeth. (tongue-jaw lift) • (crossed-finger method) Insert the index finger of the other hand down along the inside of their cheek to the base of the tongue. Use a hooking motion from the side of the mouth toward the center to dislodge the foreign body (see figure 5-20).

After establishing an open airway, it is important to evaluate the casualty's respirations and maintain that airway in an open position. This is the "R" of MARCH-PAWS. Respiratory distress means difficulty breathing (rapid or abnormally slow breathing), in other words, it is difficult for the casualty to get air in or out. Airway and respiration are not addressed in CUF; however, they must be addressed in TFC.

The pleural space between the lungs and chest wall naturally has negative pressure, which helps the lungs to collapse (exhale) and expand (inhale). With either a blunt or penetrating injury to the chest wall or lungs, air may counteract the lung's natural tendency to expand and collapse. This is due to positive pressure replacing negative pressure. It results in air being trapped in the pleural space, putting pressure on the affected lung. This forces the lungs to collapse and reduces the ability to get oxygen to the body.

While it may be easy to see a gunshot wound or shrapnel wound to the chest, it is important to evaluate casualties for additional injuries from blunt force trauma which may have been caused from an explosive device or from the chest hitting the steering wheel during a high-impact vehicle accident.

Signs of future life-threatening respiration issues include bruising, contusions (swelling around the chest, back, or rib cage), crepitus (crackling, popping, grating) that are felt or heard, or other deformities of the chest not normally seen without removing the clothing. Signs of respiratory distress include: • Difficulty in breathing. • Struggling to get air in and out. • Breathing is too weak to be effective (less than six times per minute). • Rapid breathing (greater than 20 times per minute). Note. The above signs may also indicate a penetrating chest wound injury. Report findings of respiratory distress to medical personnel.

In TCCC, various specialized equipment is used to address respiration and breathing control in combat situations. These tools are designed to promptly manage compromised airways and provide respiratory support. The primary equipment used includes: • NPA. • BVM. • Chest Seal. • 10–14-gauge catheter over needle device.

An NPA is a flexible tube inserted through the nose into the oropharynx to maintain an open airway and facilitate adequate breathing. It is particularly useful when there is a risk of tongue obstruction or in cases where the patient is conscious and able to maintain their own airway.

A BVM device consists of a self-inflating bag and a mask that is manually squeezed to deliver positive pressure ventilation. It is used when there is a need for artificial respiration to support or control the patient's breathing.

A chest seal is an airtight dressing that is applied over a penetrating chest wound to prevent the entry of air into the pleural cavity, reducing the risk of a tension pneumothorax. It allows for the restoration of normal respiratory function by maintaining appropriate chest pressure. The CoTCCC-recommended chest seal is a vented (preferred) self-adhering chest seal (see figure 6-1 on page 74) is used for treating and sucking chest wounds or open pneumothorax. 73

The equipment is essential components of TCCC's approach to respiration and breathing control. Utilizing this equipment enables military personnel to manage airway obstructions, provide respiratory support, and prevent potentially life-threatening complications associated with compromised breathing in combat scenarios.

The CoTCCC-recommended catheter-over-needle device is used to treat tension pneumothorax. The recommended catheter-over-needle device is either a 10-gauge, 14-gauge, or 3¼ inch long device (see figure 6-2). TIER 1 SKILLS FOR RESPIRATION AND BREATHING CONTROL 20B

Often the act of just opening and maintaining the airway will allow the casualty to breathe properly. The first responder opens the casualty's airway maintaining the head position to keep the airway open. Failure to maintain the open airway will prevent the casualty from receiving an adequate supply of oxygen. While maintaining an open airway the first responder checks for breathing, respiration rate (breaths per minute) and respiration quality (shallow and labored) by placing the casualty on their back and assessing their breathing by observing the casualty's chest by— • Looking for the chest to rise and fall. • Listening for air escaping during exhalation by placing your ear near the casualty's mouth. • Feeling for the flow of air on your cheek (see figure 6-3). 74 Respiration and Breathing Control

If air is not flowing freely in and out, the first responder opens the airway maneuvers as described in paragraphs 5-16 through 5-21. Note. If the casualty has a suspected neck or spine injury, and the situation allows, use, and maintain the jaw-thrust maneuver.

If the casualty is unconscious, and the respiratory rate is less than two in 15 seconds, or the casualty is making snoring or gurgling sounds, the first responder inserts an NPA by— • Keeping the casualty in a face-up position. • Lubricating the tube of the NPA with water. • Pushing the tip of the casualty's nose upward gently. • Positioning the tube of the NPA so that the bevel (pointed end) of the NPA faces toward the septum (the partition inside the nose that separates the nostrils). • Inserting the NPA into the nostril and advance it until the flange rests against the nostril. Most NPAs are designed to be placed in the right nostril.

The first responder places the casualty in the recovery position by rolling the casualty as a single unit onto their side, placing the casualty's hand of the upper arm under the casualty's chin, and flexing the casualty's upper leg. The first responder then watches the casualty closely for life-threatening conditions and checks for other injuries.

If the casualty is not breathing, immediately start rescuing breathing and seek medical aid. If the casualty resumes breathing at any time during this procedure, the airway is kept open, and the casualty is continued to be watched. If the casualty continues to breathe, they should be transported to medical aid, or to an MTF IAW the tactical situation.

Exposure to smoke or toxic inhalants can cause difficulty breathing, but other injuries can also lead to respiratory distress. Life-threatening chest injuries can also result in respiratory distress. There are two types of chest injuries that can potentially be life-threatening, penetrating injuries, like those seen in gunshot or shrapnel wounds, or blunt trauma from blasts or vehicular accidents. It is important to roll the casualty to examine the front and back for signification torso trauma. 75

At this point in the MARCH-PAWS protocol, the responder's role is to carefully roll the casualty to examine both the front and back of the torso for any signs of chest trauma. It is crucial for the responder to identify and acknowledge if the casualty has a potentially life-threatening chest injury that is causing respiratory distress. The responder must then effectively communicate these findings to the medical personnel arriving on the scene, ensuring that the casualty receives the appropriate medical attention promptly.

The Tier 2 skills do not replace all Service member skills for respiration and breathing control. The CLS must reassess respiration and breathing control in TFC and start more advanced respiration and breathing control interventions. The CLS must be ready to treat an open pneumothorax, a tension pneumothorax, and identify if the treatment for those injuries was successful.
An open pneumothorax is also known as a sucking chest wound. An open pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space. The pleural space is the thin area between the lungs and chest wall.

When a casualty experiences penetrating torso trauma the elastic lung deflates and pulls away from the chest wall. If the hole, through the chest wall, is at least the size of a nickel or 2/3 the diameter of the trachea, on inspiration, the air now enters the chest through the hole instead of into the lungs through the normal airways of the mouth and nose. As a result, the affected lung cannot be fully re-inflated by inhalation.
An open pneumothorax usually occurs with a hole in the chest the size of a nickel or bigger. Not all chest wounds are sucking chest wounds; some do not penetrate as deeply as the lung cavity.

The first responders check the casualty's respiration and ability to breathe. All open or sucking chest wounds are treated by immediately applying a vented chest seal to cover the defect. If a determination cannot be made if the wound has penetrated the chest wall completely, treat the wound as though it were an open chest wound. A casualty with an open chest wound will exhibit one or more of the following signs and symptoms: • A "sucking" or "hissing" sound when the casualty inhales. • Difficulty breathing. • A puncture wound of the chest. • Froth or bubbles around the injury. • Coughing up blood. • Blood-tinged sputum (spit).

For respiratory distress not resolved by a chest seal or in a casualty with known or suspected chest or back trauma without an open sucking chest wound, consider a tension pneumothorax, and perform a needle decompression of the chest (NDC). Injuries to the chest are very serious and can be life-threatening. The casualty's condition can change quickly with a chest injury.

An open chest wound should be treated with a CoTCCCrecommended commercial chest seal found within the first aid kit, which maybe vented or non-vented. Vented chest seals are for treating penetrating wounds to the chest. The vented chest seals allow air to escape out of the chest while non-vented chest seals do not. The injured lung will remain partially collapsed, but the mechanics of respiration will be better.

Recommended treatment for open or sucking chest wounds is prompt application of a vented chest seal. If a vented chest seal is NOT available, a non-vented chest seal should be used. When the casualty inhales, 76 Respiration and Breathing Control the plastic is sucked against the wound, preventing the entry of air. When the casualty exhales, trapped air can escape from the wound and out the valve.

The wound should be uncovered unless clothing is stuck to the wound or in a CBRN environment. Once an open wound is discovered, place a gloved hand over the wound to provide a temporary seal. Note. If unsure that the wound has penetrated the chest wall completely, treat the wound as though it were an open chest wound. If multiple wounds are found, treat as soon as they are discovered. First wound found; first wound treated.

Fully open the outer wrapper of the casualty's commercial chest seal located in the casualty's first aid kit. Wipe any dirt, blood, or sweat from the skin with gauze supplied in the commercial chest seal. Instruct the casualty to fully exhale and then immediately place the vent of the chest seal directly over the first wound encountered. Do not touch the inner adhesive surface of the commercial chest seal. Ensure that the edges of the chest seal extend two inches beyond the wound. Firmly press the chest seal on the skin to ensure a good airtight seal. If the chest seal does not provide a good airtight seal, apply a two-inch tape (from the casualty's first aid kit) to all four sides of the chest seal, ensuring the tape does not cover any vents, and secure it firmly to the casualty's chest.

Roll the casualty on their side or have the conscious casualty sit up and examine their back for any wounds. If any wounds are present on the back, treat as a chest injury with a commercial chest seal. Encourage the casualty to breathe normally. Place the casualty in a position of comfort (usually sitting) if conscious, or in the recovery position (on the casualty's side), with the injured side down if unconscious. Continue to monitor the casualty for signs of respiratory distress (increased difficulty breathing). If the casualty has increased difficulty breathing, lift the chest seal, release any trapped air by wiping blood or debris from the wound, and reseal or replace the chest seal upon exhalation. Seek medical aid and continue to monitor the casualty until relieved by medical personnel.

Tension pneumothorax is caused by significant torso (chest) trauma, or a blast injury resulting in severe and progressive respiratory distress. Progressive difficulty breathing is labored, and rapid breathing worsens overtime.

A tension pneumothorax is the second-leading cause of preventable deaths on the battlefield. As a tension pneumothorax develops, air enters the chest cavity through the wound with every inspiration but does not leave with expiration and is trapped. Every breath adds more air to the air space inside the rib cage and outside the lung, and the pressure inside the chest builds up (figure 6-4). 77

When a lung is injured, it can act like a one-way valve, trapping air between the lung and chest wall. This trapped air builds pressure, potentially compressing both lungs and the heart, impairing their function and leading to respiratory distress and shock. In tension pneumothorax, this elevated pressure stops the lungs and heart from expanding normally, which can be fatal. Signs of tension pneumothorax vary from early to late stages: • Early signs include: ▪ Increasing difficulty breathing over time. ▪ Shortness of breath. ▪ Confusion, lightheadedness, or agitation from low oxygen. ▪ Bluish discoloration around the mouth and lips. ▪ Rapid pulse. • Late signs, which may appear as the condition worsens, include: ▪ Swollen neck veins. ▪ Tracheal deviation (the windpipe shifting to one side). ▪ Severe difficulty breathing, often with chest pain or anxiety.
These signs might be hard to detect in a combat situation. Responders must be vigilant for tension pneumothorax if there is any chest wound accompanied by increasing breathing difficulties.

It's crucial to monitor these signs during TFC. Like controlling bleeding, treating a tension pneumothorax is crucial; if left untreated, it can lead to severe respiratory issues, shock, and death. The initial treatment for a suspected tension pneumothorax is NDC. After this, any chest injury, whether an open pneumothorax or tension pneumothorax, needs further evaluation by medical personnel and likely evacuation

sections.section: Unsuccessful treatment or recurrence of tension pneumothorax
sections.text: Casualties with a tension pneumothorax must be continuously monitored for reoccurring symptoms. The condition may initially be treated unsuccessfully and then spontaneously recur. The immediate remedy for the unsuccessful treatment or recurrence of a tension pneumothorax is to burp the chest seal, if one is in place.

sections.section: Unsuccessful treatment or recurrence of tension pneumothorax
sections.text: If initial treatment of tension pneumothorax with NDC does not result in improvement, a second NDC should be attempted at the alternate recommended site. If tension pneumothorax initially responds to NDC, but symptoms later recur, then repeat NDC at the same site right beside the original NDC. If no improvement is noted after the second NDC, proceed with circulation assessment and treatment following the MARCHPAWS protocol. 78 Respiration and Breathing Control

The treatment is to let the air trapped under pressure escape by inserting an NDC into the chest. The NDC site selection is based on the mechanism of injury and the physical findings during the tactical trauma assessment. The NDC (see figure 6-5 below) is placed either at the— • Second, intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line. • If the needle is used at the second intercostal space, ensure the site selection is outside the nipple line. • Anterior axillary line in the fifth intercostal space.

The NDC should be placed perpendicular to the body. After the NDC is placed, the needle should be held in place for 5-10 seconds before removing the needle and leaving the catheter. As with all other treatment given, it is critical to document all interventions on DD Form 1380.

After the casualty has been treated with an NDC, the casualty should be placed in the position of comfort. If the casualty is unconscious, place the casualty in the recovery position. If the casualty is conscious, allow the casualty to adopt the sitting position, if breathing is more comfortable.

Expedient techniques for respiration and breathing control in TCCC are crucial for immediate and effective management of a compromised casualty in combat situations. These techniques are designed to be quickly implemented by military personnel with minimal equipment, providing life-saving interventions in high-stress and time-critical environments. Expedient techniques may include maneuvers such as the head-tilt/chin-lift or jaw-thrust to open the airway, clearing obstructing objects, or repositioning the casualty to optimize breathing. Additionally, rescue breaths or mouth-to-mouth ventilation can be employed to support respiration. These expedient techniques are crucial time until advanced medical care can be provided, ensuring that the injured Service members receive immediate attention to maintain adequate respiration and oxygenation, thereby increasing their chances of survival in the challenging conditions of the battlefield. 79

Penetrating chest injuries involve the intrusion of foreign objects such as bullets, knives, or projectiles through the chest wall, penetrating into the thoracic cavity. This breach can lead to severe damage to vital structures including the lungs, heart, major blood vessels, or other organs within the thoracic cavity.

Penetrating chest injuries can result in significant internal bleeding, pneumothorax (collapsed lung), hemothorax (accumulation of blood in the chest cavity), tension pneumothorax (air buildup under pressure in the chest), or cardiac tamponade (compression of the heart due to blood accumulation). They are considered severe and life-threatening, requiring immediate intervention to stabilize the casualty and prevent further complications. Penetrating chest injuries can also be referred to as an open chest wound.

A CoTCCC vented commercial chest seal is the preferred type of chest seal. However, if one is unavailable, a non-vented commercial chest seal may be applied in the same manner as a vented commercial chest seal. If there is not a commercial chest seal available, the following examples can be used as occlusive (airtight) materials: • Plastics such as the outer wrapper of the emergency dressing from the first aid kit. • The combat ration packing. • Cellophane.

An improvised chest seal may be used to treat an open chest wound by— • Wiping any dirt, blood, or sweat from the skin with gauze or any available clothing. • Instructing the casualty to fully exhale and then place the inner surface of the outer wrapper or other occlusive material directly over the wound. Note. Do not touch the inner surface of the occlusive material. Ensure that the edges of the occlusive material extend two inches beyond the wound. • • • • • Applying two-inch tape from the casualty's first aid kit to three sides of the occlusive material and secure it firmly to the casualty's chest. Leave the side nearest to the ground un-taped. Rolling the casualty on their side or have the conscious casualty sit up and examine the back for any wounds. Checking the casualty for any wounds on the back and treating it as a chest injury with a large improvised occlusive chest seal (such as the plastic wrapper from the emergency dressing in the first aid kit). Placing the casualty in a position of comfort (usually sitting) if conscious, or in the recovery position (on the casualty's side) with the injured side down if unconscious. Continuing to monitor the casualty for signs of respiratory distress (increased difficulty breathing). Note. If the casualty has increased difficulty breathing, lift the chest seal, release any trapped air by wiping blood or debris from the wound, and reseal or replace the chest seal upon exhalation.

External chest compressions, also known as Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR), in combat casualties is nearly always the result of hemorrhagic or obstructive shock, neither of which will respond to standard CPR. Conducting CPR may delay definitive treatment in nearly all cases. The CoTCCC guidelines recommend performing bilateral needle decompression and expedite blood product administration. Mission variables or the credentialed provider may guide exceptions to this rule in support of CPR on combat casualties. The administration of CPR on a combat casualty should be a rare circumstance and not the standard of care in this trauma population.

CPR is conducted using a specific technique to provide manual circulation support during cardiac arrest or when the heart has stopped beating effectively. A general outline of the steps involved in conducting external chest compressions is: • Position: Ensure the person is lying on a firm, flat surface, such as the ground or a CPR board. Kneel beside the person's chest. 80 Respiration and Breathing Control • • • • • • Hand Placement: Place the heel of one hand on the center of the person's chest, between the nipples. For infants or children, use two or three fingers instead of the entire hand. Compression Depth: Press down firmly and smoothly. For adults, compress the chest at least two inches (five centimeters) deep. For infants or children, compress the chest about one-third to onehalf of its depth. Compression Rate: Perform compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. This equates to about two compressions per second. Complete Chest Recoil: Allow the chest to fully recoil between each compression, without lifting your hands off the chest. This allows the heart to refill with blood. Compression to Ventilation Ratio: If you are performing CPR alone, do cycles of 30 chest compressions to two rescue breaths (mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-mask). If there are two rescuers, the ratio can be 30:2 or continuous chest compressions with ventilation being delivered by the other rescuer. Continue until Help Arrives: Keep performing chest compressions until professional medical help arrives, or until the person shows signs of movement or starts breathing.

It is important to note that these steps provide a general overview of external chest compressions. Proper CPR training and certification are needed to gain a thorough understanding of the technique and to ensure accurate and effective application during emergency situations.

The duration of CPR can vary depending on the circumstances and response of the individual being treated. In general, CPR should be continued until one of the following conditions is met: • Signs of Life: If the person shows obvious signs of life, such as breathing normally, coughing, or moving, CPR can be stopped. • Professional Medical Help Arrives: CPR should be continued until professional medical personnel take over the resuscitation efforts. • Provider Fatigue: If the person performing CPR becomes too exhausted to continue effectively, they can switch with another trained individual to maintain the quality of compression.

In many cases, CPR is performed continuously without interruptions until one of the above conditions is met. However, it is important to note that high-quality chest compressions are crucial for improving the chances of survival. Therefore, proper training in CPR techniques and regular updates on the latest guidelines are recommended to ensure effective and efficient resuscitation efforts.

Rescue breathing, also known as artificial ventilation, is a technique used in CPR to provide oxygen to a person who is not breathing or has inadequate breathing. It involves delivering breaths into the person's lungs to support their respiratory function. Rescue breathing is conducted executing the following: • Position: Ensure the casualty is lying on a flat surface, preferably with their head tilted back slightly to open the airway. • Clear the Airway: Check for any visible obstructions in the person's mouth or throat, and if present, gently remove them if possible. • Seal the Mouth: If the casualty's mouth is open, use your hand to gently lift the chin upward to maintain an open airway. With your other hand, pinch the person's nose closed to prevent air from escaping. • Breathing Technique: Place your mouth over the casualty's mouth, forming a seal, and blow into their mouth while watching for the chest to rise. Deliver the breath over one second and make sure it is sufficient to visibly inflate the chest. • Breathing Rate: Provide rescue breaths at a rate of about one breath every five to six seconds (10 to 12 breaths per minute). • Chest Recoil: Allow the chest to fully recoil between breaths. This enables the chest to return to its resting position, which helps in the exchange of gases during respiration. • Continue Until Help Arrives: Perform rescue breathing until professional medical help arrives or until the person starts breathing on their own.

There are several methods for rescue breathing, each suitable for different situations and age groups. The main methods include: 81 • • • • Mouth-to-Mouth: This common method involves the rescuer forming a seal over the casualty's mouth with their own and delivering breaths into their lungs. Mouth-to-Nose: Used when the casualty's mouth is injured, obstructed, or inaccessible, the rescuer closes the casualty's mouth and breathes into their nose to create a seal. Mouth-to-Mask: In situations like professional CPR or with specialized equipment, a pocket mask or BVM device is used. The mask covers the casualty's mouth and nose, and the rescuer delivers breaths by squeezing the bag or using the valve. Mouth-to-Stoma: For individuals with a tracheostomy or a surgical stoma in the neck for breathing, rescue breaths can be delivered directly into the stoma using the rescuer's mouth or a specialized device.

It is important to note that the technique and ratio of rescue breaths may vary depending on the age of the person receiving CPR (such as an adult, child, or infant) and the specific guidelines in the area or operation. Proper training in CPR techniques, including rescue breathing, is crucial to ensure accurate and effective administration of artificial ventilation during emergency situations.

It is important to follow the specific guidelines and protocols for rescue breathing based on the person's age, condition, and the resources available. Proper training and certification in CPR techniques are essential to gain proficiency in rescue breathing and to ensure the best possible outcomes during resuscitation efforts. 82

Hemorrhage control assessment and management in TFC falls under the "C," for Circulation, in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. The body requires good blood flow throughout, and a lack of good blood flow may cause the casualty to go into hypovolemic shock.

Hemorrhage control in the TFC phase takes place after massive bleeding control that occurs in the CUF phase. It is possible that it did not occur, and this may be the first opportunity to address massive bleeding as well, so there is significant urgency. The first step is to reassess all prior hemorrhage control interventions for effectiveness.

The casualty's hemorrhage control interventions must be frequently reassessed to ensure continued hemorrhage control. This includes reassessments at frequent time intervals and any time the casualty is moved or the casualty's status changes. The casualty must be continually watched for signs of shock.

Controlling shock is the primary method of circulation control. Shock is the inadequate blood flow to body tissues. Inadequate blood volume inside the circulatory system results in inadequate oxygen delivery to the body's cells. As cells, tissues, and organs cease to function, eventually the whole body will fail, and death follows. Note. Hypovolemic shock can also result from blood loss due to internal bleeding into the abdominal or chest cavity. The first responder or CLS will not be able to control internal bleeding. This condition requires rapid evacuation of the casualty.

Shock is caused by a decrease in the amount of blood volume circulating in the casualty's blood circulatory system. Shocks can have many causes such as: • Low blood volume or hypovolemia (such as dehydration or blood loss). • Low blood pressure. • Heart failure (pump failure). • Neurologic damage (infection, allergic reaction). • Obstructive causes (such as tension pneumothorax or pericardial tamponade causes obstruction of the heart).

Shock is usually caused by severe bleeding, but it can also be caused by severe burns classified as partial thickness burns (2nd degree) or full thickness burns (3rd degree) on 20 percent or more of the body surface. On the battlefield, assume shock is from severe blood loss (also called hemorrhagic shock). The signs and symptoms of shock include: • Mental confusion. • Weak or absent radial pulse. • Rapid breathing. • Nausea. • Sweaty, cool, or clammy skin. • Excessive thirst. • Pale or gray skin. • Previous severe bleeding 83 IMPORTANT! Alert medical personnel if the casualty is presenting signs of shock.

If the casualty has both indicators of mental confusion and weak or absent radial pulse of shock, the casualty has lost a significant amount of blood. Shock will lead to the casualty's death if not quickly recognized and treated. Table 7-1 provides an overview of the effects of blood loss and highlights why it is important to quickly apply a TQ during CUF, reassess, and evaluate for additional bleeding sources during TFC.

It is more effective to prevent shock through hemorrhage control than to treat it once it has developed. Even in cases where shock is already present, the most critical first action is to control any bleeding. Continuously reassess all bleeding control measures, such as tourniquets and pressure dressings, to ensure they remain effective and are adjusted tightly as soon as possible. This is a crucial step in treating shock.

Internal bleeding caused by blunt or penetrating trauma to the chest or abdomen may not be immediately controlled and can lead to shock later on. Continuous assessment of the casualty is essential. Even if a casualty is not currently in shock but has sustained serious injuries, they should be carefully monitored for signs of developing shock. It's important not to wait until signs and symptoms of shock appear. While medical personnel will provide comprehensive treatments, controlling any external bleeding early can save valuable time.

At present, no specialized equipment has been designated exclusively for managing circulation control. The equipment mentioned in the earlier section of this publication serves to support and enhance circulation control measures. 84 Circulation Control TIER 1 SKILLS FOR CIRCULATION CONTROL 25B

The best way to prevent shock is to control bleeding. Responders should continuously monitor and reassess the effectiveness of bleeding control measures to ensure they are working, TQ application, wound packing with hemostatic dressing, a pressure dressing, or a combination of these.

After reassessing TQs and hemostatic dressings, the TCCC guideline on shock states: "Assess for hemorrhagic shock" (altered mental status in the absence of brain injury or weak and absent radial pulse). Reassess all bleeding control measures are still effective and TQs remain tight.
Control bleeding and then take steps to prevent shock by elevating the casualty's legs higher than the casualty's heart if their airway tolerates lying flat on their back.

Conduct a bleeding re-check by: • Reassess every TQ and dressing that may have been applied earlier. • Expose the area and determine if bleeding is controlled. • Expose and clearly mark all TQ sites with the time of TQ application if not previously done. • When time and the tactical situation permit, check for further bleeding, and for pulses further out on the limb than the TQ.

Move the casualty under a permanent or improvised shelter to shade them from direct sunlight. If the casualty is conscious, place the casualty in the shock recovery position (see figure 7-1), which is on their back with their feet elevated slightly above the level of their heart. This will help their blood circulation. A log, field pack, box, rolled field jacket, or other stable objects can be used to elevate their feet. If a sitting position makes it easier for the casualty to breathe, that is fine.
The following steps will also significantly help in the prevention of shock: • Loosen clothing at the neck, waist, or anywhere is binding.

When providing first aid for shock, DO NOT give the casualty any food or drink. If you must leave the casualty or if they are unconscious, turn their head to the side (see figure 7-2) to prevent them from choking, if they vomit.

Tier 2 skills for this section specifically address the crucial aspect of circulation control. Emphasizing the need for rapid and appropriate interventions to prevent further harm and optimize the chances of survival for wounded Service members. Circulation control involves techniques and procedures aimed at managing bleeding and vascular injuries. These are often encountered in high-stakes and dynamic combat environments.

Pelvic fractures can be a cause of massive internal bleeding and impact circulation, which is the "C" in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. A pelvic fracture may be suspected if the casualty's injuries are a result of blunt force or blast trauma with one or more of the following: • Pelvic pain. • Major lower-limb amputation or lower-limb near amputations. • Pelvic deformities, penetrating injuries, or bruising near the pelvis. • Pelvic instability or crepitus, which is a crinkly, grating feeling, or sound under the skin. • Unconsciousness or shock.

If a pelvic fracture is suspected, the casualty will require advanced evaluation by medical personnel, and you should notify medical personnel of the potential for a pelvic fracture as soon as possible. 86 Circulation Control

The regular reassessment of pressure bandages is crucial in managing wounds effectively. The CLS are tasked with ensuring that there is no ongoing bleeding from the wound site. Additionally, it's important to check for circulation below the pressure bandage by feeling for a distal pulse—that is, a pulse found below the level of the bandage.

If the skin below the bandage is cool, bluish, numb, or if the distal pulse is absent, these may be signs that the bandage is applied too tightly, potentially hindering blood flow. In such cases, the bandage should be loosened and then securely retied to ensure proper circulation is restored.

All dressings and bandages must be checked routinely, especially every time a casualty is moved. This practice helps to monitor the effectiveness of the initial treatment and to make timely adjustments as needed.

In situations where a pressure bandage or hemostatic dressing fails to control bleeding, a TQ should be applied approximately two to three inches above the site of bleeding, if feasible. If placing a TQ is not possible and the existing bandage is either ineffective or saturated with blood, replace it with a fresh hemostatic dressing. Ensure to pack the wound thoroughly with the hemostatic material, applying constant, direct pressure at the bleeding source for optimal effectiveness.

Medical personnel may not always be readily available. Nonmedical personnel must rely on themselves, other Service members' knowledge, fundamentals of first aid for circulation control, until medical assistance arrives. This section will provide additional first aid, non-TCCC, procedures that nonmedical personnel can use for circulation control.

When medical personnel are not immediately available, non-medical personnel must depend on themselves and the knowledge of other Service members. The fundamentals of first aid for controlling circulation are crucial until professional medical help arrives. This section aims to provide essential, nonTCCC first aid procedures that non-medical personnel can use effectively to maintain circulation control.

Non-medical personnel are often the first responders in critical situations, making it essential for them to be familiar with basic first aid techniques. Understanding and applying these methods can be lifesaving when delays in professional medical treatment occur. Training in these expedient techniques empowers individuals to act confidently and efficiently, providing critical care in emergencies.

The guidance provided here includes several key first aid actions that non-medical personnel can take to manage circulation issues effectively. These include methods to minimize bleeding, stabilize the affected individual, and prepare for the arrival of medical professionals. Each technique has been chosen for its simplicity and effectiveness, ensuring that those with minimal medical training can apply them under pressure.

It is vital for all personnel, especially those in high-risk environments, to be trained in these techniques. Such training ensures that every member of a team can provide essential care in emergencies, enhancing overall safety and increasing the likelihood of positive outcomes in critical situations.

Anaphylactic shock is a severe and life-threatening allergic reaction that significantly impacts the circulatory system. This medical emergency is marked by a swift release of histamines and other chemicals into the body, leading to vasodilation and increased permeability in blood vessels. Such changes can disrupt the adequate perfusion of vital organs and tissues, putting the casualty's life at great risk.

Vasodilation, a key feature of anaphylactic shock, involves the relaxation of smooth muscle cells within blood vessel walls, causing these vessels to widen and blood pressure to drop significantly. This physiological process can rapidly deteriorate the casualty's condition.

The treatment of anaphylactic shock is urgent and time sensitive. Immediate actions include calling for medical help and, if available, using the casualty's epinephrine auto-injector. Anaphylactic reactions can 87 manifest within seconds or minutes after exposure to an allergen, affecting the skin, respiratory, and circulatory systems.

Prompt recognition and response to anaphylactic shock are critical. Assessing both the signs and symptoms early on is essential for effective intervention. Quick and accurate identification of the condition allows for the necessary steps to be taken to mitigate its life-threatening effects.

To effectively check for anaphylactic shock, Service members should follow a systematic approach: • Assess Symptoms: ▪ Observe for sudden and severe symptoms like difficulty breathing, wheezing, or shortness of breath. ▪ Check for a rapid or weak pulse. ▪ Look for swelling of the face, lips, or tongue. ▪ Note any hives or widespread skin redness. ▪ Be alert to signs of confusion, dizziness, or loss of consciousness. • Ask Questions: ▪ Inquire about any known allergies or recent exposures to potential allergens. ▪ Ask if they have ingested or come into contact with a known allergen recently. • Observe Breathing: ▪ Check for signs of respiratory distress, such as rapid or labored breathing. ▪ Listen for wheezing or other abnormal breathing sounds. • Check Circulation: ▪ Assess the pulse to determine its rate and strength. ▪ Look for signs of poor circulation, such as pale or bluish skin. • Look for Other Symptoms: ▪ Be aware of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or a feeling of impending doom.

If anaphylactic shock is suspected, immediate medical assistance is crucial. The primary treatment involves administering epinephrine (adrenaline). If an epinephrine auto-injector is available, assist the affected individual in using it, or administer it yourself if you are allowed and trained. Dosage guidelines are typically provided with the injector—0.15 milligrams (mg) for children and 0.3 mg for adults weighing more than 66 pounds.

Further doses of epinephrine may be necessary, administered every 5 to 10 minutes if prescribed and symptoms persist. Additionally, provide supportive measures for treating shock, respiratory failure, circulatory collapse, or cardiac arrest: • Position the casualty supine with legs elevated if injuries permit. • Perform rescue breathing and external chest compressions if required. • Monitor vital signs every three to five minutes until the casualty is stable.

Record all first aid actions on DD Form 1380 and request MEDEVAC immediately. Use CASEVAC only if MEDEVAC is unavailable and transport the casualty to the nearest MTF as soon as possible. Anaphylaxis is life-threatening, and immediate action is crucial. Seek professional medical help promptly and provide supportive care while awaiting arrival of medical personnel. 88

The "H" in MARCH-PAWS stands for hypothermia prevention. Hypothermia begins when the body's core temperature drops below 97° Fahrenheit (F). It can be mild (93-96°F), moderate (89-93°F), or severe (less than 89°F), depending on the temperature. To accurately diagnose hypothermia, the core temperature must be measured rectally with a special low-range thermometer, as mouth and ear measurements won't work well in cold environments.

Hypothermia can be caused by being in a cold environment or by losing a lot of blood, a condition known as hypovolemia. This is when there's a significant drop in the volume of blood circulating in the body. Both environmental exposure and loss of blood can lead to dangerously low body temperatures, which can be life-threatening if not treated.

Environmental hypothermia happens when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it, often from being in cold weather for too long. Hypothermia from hypovolemic shock happens due to a large loss of blood or fluids, making it hard for the body to keep warm. Both causes can lead to serious health issues, including death, if not managed quickly.

Hypothermia can happen suddenly, like from falling into cold water, or slowly, if someone is exposed to cold conditions for a long time. It can even happen in mild temperatures if a person is wet, which makes it easier to lose body heat. Factors like wet clothing, not enough food, exhaustion, and drinking alcohol or using drugs can make hypothermia worse.

Massive bleeding can cause hypothermia, which in turn can cause more bleeding because cold temperatures can prevent blood from clotting properly. This is a problem even in warm weather, and especially for people in shock who can't generate enough body heat. It's crucial to stop this cycle to save the person's life.

In the TFC phase of care, the focus has shifted from immediate life-threatening hemorrhage control during CUF phase, to the reassessment of all previous interventions. This is followed by the prevention and treatment of other injuries and complications such as hypothermia. It is important to identify the signs of hypothermia. Some easily recognizable signs of hypothermia are: • Vigorous shivering is typically present. • Shivering may decrease or cease as the core temperature continues to fall. • Conscious, but usually apathetic or lethargic. • Confusion. • Sleepiness. • Slurred speech or mumbling. • Slow breathing and drowsiness. • Weak pulse. • Low or unattainable blood pressure. • Change in behavior with or without poor control over body movements, and with or without slow reactions.

The signs and symptoms of hypothermia may vary depending on the severity and can be categorized into mild, moderate, and severe stages: • Mild Hypothermia: ▪ Shivering. ▪ Cold and pale skin. ▪ Numbness or tingling in extremities. ▪ Fatigue and drowsiness. 89 • • ▪ Slurred speech. ▪ Impaired coordination and fine motor skills. Moderate Hypothermia: ▪ Intense shivering or shivering stops. ▪ Difficulty in speaking and thinking clearly. ▪ Clumsiness and lack of coordination. ▪ Cold, pale, or blue-gray skin. ▪ Slow breathing and heart rate. ▪ Weak pulse. Severe Hypothermia: ▪ Shivering may stop completely. ▪ Confusion and disorientation. ▪ Loss of consciousness. ▪ Very cold, pale, or bluish skin. ▪ Slow or irregular breathing. ▪ Weak or absent pulse.

The goals for first aid for hypothermia are to rescue, examine, insulate, and rapidly transport. If untreated, hypothermia is a true medical emergency and requires evacuation. Evacuate as soon as possible with the casualty lying down.

Re-warming techniques include— • Remove the casualty from the cold environment. • Replace wet clothing with dry clothing. • Cover the casualty with insulating material or blanket. • Wrap the casualty from head to toe. • Avoid unnecessary movement from the casualty. • If the casualty is conscious, slowly give high caloric sweet warm fluids. • Seek medical aid.

Hypothermia is a serious condition that requires professional evaluation and treatment. Attempting to rewarm a severely hypothermic person should be done by medical professionals using appropriate techniques. While waiting for help to arrive, focus on preventing further heat loss and providing support to the person.

Preventing hypothermia is critical in reducing the effects of heat loss and preventing deaths from uncontrolled bleeding. Immediate action to prevent hypothermia should commence right after an injury occurs. Without preventative measures, there is a real risk that a casualty may succumb to hemorrhage from a wound that could otherwise be survivable. As blood loss itself can lead to hypothermia, it is vital for first responders and CLS to control bleeding and actively engage in both passive and active measures to prevent the casualty's body temperature from dropping.

The quicker hypothermia prevention begins, the less severe its impact will be on the casualty's bleeding and potential shock. Minimizing exposure to the elements is essential. Actions such as replacing wet clothing with dry ones and placing the casualty on an insulated surface should be prioritized. Environmental factors such as daily temperature fluctuations, nightfall, changes in altitude, and wind exposure must also be considered as they can significantly affect body heat retention. 90 Hypothermia Control

Prevention of hypothermia is far more manageable than treating it once it has set in. Starting hypothermia prevention measures early is crucial because a decreased body temperature can adversely affect blood clotting processes, heightening the risk of continued bleeding—even in warm conditions.

CLS personnel must be proactive in assuming that every casualty is at risk of developing hypothermia, utilizing all known prevention techniques. If a casualty is already hypothermic, the response should be even more aggressive, treating the condition as a direct threat to the casualty's life.

To prevent hypothermia, it is essential to keep the casualty warm, even in very hot environments. This is particularly crucial when a casualty is suffering from hemorrhagic shock due to blood loss, as they are at an extreme risk for developing hypothermia. Both active and passive methods should be employed to ensure the casualty's body temperature is maintained. This involves proactive measures such as providing thermal blankets, using heat packs, and minimizing exposure to cold or windy conditions. Maintaining warmth not only aids in preventing hypothermia but also helps stabilize the casualty's overall condition.

The hypothermia control equipment falls into either active warming (external source of heat) or passive warming blankets, or a poncho liner to treat or prevent hypothermia. The most common equipment seen is the hypothermia prevention and management kit, blankets, or ponchos.

Medical personnel will distribute active hypothermia blankets based on the unit mission and load. Active hypothermia blankets are activated when their heating elements are exposed to air and can produce temperatures reaching 104° F for up to eight hours. Active hypothermia blankets are applied to a casualty who cannot generate their own heat, but not directly on their skin, because the activated blankets can cause burns.

Apply the active warming blanket from the active hypothermia materials to the casualty's torso, not directly on the skin, and cover the casualty with the passive hypothermia shell. Continue to reassess the casualty to determine if additional methods are needed to prevent or treat hypothermia. The heat reflective shell will help to retain the heat produced by the ready-heat blanket. It has an incorporated hood and Velcro closures down each side to allow exposure of an arm or a leg. Such exposure allows the medic to attend to IVs and TQs.

If an active hypothermia device is not available, a combination of the passive warming blanket and active warming blanket may be used. Active hypothermia treatment uses heating sources such as the readyheat blanket to warm the casualty. This requires a chemical reaction with oxygen, so at higher altitudes there may not be enough oxygen to sustain the chemical reaction required to generate heat.

You must determine based on the environmental conditions whether the casualty needs both the outer shell and the heating blanket. It is sufficient to just keep them covered with the shell, because it is already hot outside.

If no active rewarming equipment is available, then use passive warming devices that will retain heat and keep the casualty dry. The casualty should be assessed for hemorrhagic shock and ensure bleeding is controlled. WARNING: Active warming is contraindicated in a casualty who is showing signs and symptoms of hyperthermia from heat related illness. 91

Passive hypothermia blankets are designed to retain the casualty's body heat by enclosing them within a thermal barrier, keeping them off the cold ground. While passive strategies prevent further cooling, they do not actively warm the casualty. Therefore, it's critical to avoid placing the casualty directly onto cold, wet, or damp surfaces; instead, a blanket or poncho should be positioned underneath them to provide insulation. In the absence of specialized re-warming equipment, dry blankets, poncho liners, sleeping bags, or similar items should be used to retain heat and keep the casualty dry and elevated from the ground.

Key considerations include recognizing that blood loss can significantly reduce body temperature, even in warmer climates. When using a blanket or any passive heating material, it is crucial to wrap the casualty completely, including their head, but ensure the face remains uncovered to prevent breathing obstructions. Leaving any part of the body exposed can result in heat loss and worsen hypothermia. These measures are vital in managing a hypothermic casualty, especially in the absence of active warming tools.

sections.section: TIER 1 SKILLS USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
sections.text: The first responder must prevent, and address hypothermia compounded by massive blood loss. This is not hypothermia due to cold weather, but can be prevented by— • Keeping clothing or uniform on the casualty. • Replacing extremely wet clothing if possible and keeping the casualty dry. • Keeping the casualty off the ground, by placing a barrier between the casualty and the ground or lifting them off the ground, if possible. Note. Contact with the ground increases loss of body heat. • • Using dry blankets, poncho liners, sleeping bags, or anything that will retain heat. Minimizing the casualty's exposure to the environment.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS USED FOR HYPOTHERMIA CONTROL
sections.text: The Tier 2 TCCC skills emphasize advanced yet practical approaches to managing battlefield casualties under hypothermic conditions. Personnel trained in Tier 2 TCCC are equipped with the knowledge and skills to effectively use available medical equipment to prevent and treat hypothermia. This includes the application of specialized gear such as hypothermia prevention and management kits, which are designed to maintain body temperature and prevent further heat loss in injured soldiers. In addition, Tier 2 personnel are trained to monitor vital signs closely, ensuring that the core body temperature is maintained within a safe range, thereby reducing the risk of hypothermia-related complications.

sections.section: Expedient skills used for hypothermia control
sections.text: In situations where standard medical supplies are not available, field expedient techniques for hypothermia control become crucial. Soldiers are taught to use their environment and available resources to prevent and manage hypothermia. For instance, using space blankets or even regular blankets to wrap the victim can significantly reduce heat loss. If these are not available, utilizing materials such as leaves, grass, or even newspapers as insulation can be a life-saving improvisation. Creating a barrier between the victim and the cold ground, such as with a sleeping pad, backpack, or any available material, can also prevent further body heat loss. These improvised methods are essential skills in TCCC, enabling soldiers to provide effective hypothermia care even in resource-limited settings. 92 Wounds, Splinting and Mechanism of Injury, Injury Type, Signs and Symptoms, and Treatments

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
