sections.text: As discussed in paragraph 3-96 on page 39, PAWS is the second part of the MARCH-PAWS casualty assessment and is conducted after the MARCH portion. The MIST reporting was introduced as a standard component of the MEDEVAC request during Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: While not officially part of the NATO and U.S. standard MEDEVAC request, MIST reporting has become customary in some operations. Often referred to as the 10th line in the 9-line MEDEVAC request, the completed DD Form 1380 serves as the MIST report. However, the high volume of casualties expected during large scale combat operations may make it challenging to complete MIST reporting for each casualty.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: The MIST report facilitates the transfer of medical information to the receiving health care provider by providing a structured approach to the casualty handoff. A MIST report delivers additional evacuation information that might be required by theater commanders and assists the receiving MTF in preparing for specific inbound casualties. However, transmitting a MIST report for each casualty during operations and mass casualty incidents may not always be timely or feasible.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: The combat wound medication pack (CWMP) is both the "P" (pain) and the "A" (antibiotics) in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. Pain is common with battlefield injuries. Some injuries and levels of pain can be treated safely by using pain medications (also known as analgesics) in the CWMP. These include fractures, burns, and eye injuries.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: The CWMP is a prepackaged medication packet with drugs and dosages specifically chosen for use in combat casualty care. The CWMP contains drugs for mild to moderate pain (Meloxicam and Acetaminophen) and an antibiotic specific for penetrating wounds (Moxifloxacin). The CWMP should be used only for combat related injuries and is not for routine use. It may be procured through medical logistics systems as a prepackaged blister pack or, may be locally packaged by medical personnel.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: For pain relief on the battlefield of mild to moderate pain that will not keep the casualty out of the fight, ensure they take their CWMP. The casualty should take all three medications in the CWMP. This can give significant pain relief and will not alter the casualty's mental status. This is a good option when the casualty's pain and wounds are not severe enough to keep them out of the fight. Note. If the casualty has wounds or pain severe enough to render them unable to fight, then medical personnel have other options for more effective pain relief. The medications given by medical personnel will generally require that the casualty be disarmed because the medications can alter the casualty's mental status.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: CWMP is a prepackaged pill pack containing CoTCCC-recommended medications for use in combat casualty care. The CWMP is found in the casualty's first aid kit. It contains medications for pain and antibiotics that can be taken by mouth.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: The medication in the CWMP should be taken as soon as possible after life-threatening conditions have been addressed. All medications administered should be documented along with the time given on the DD Form 1380. 93

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: The CWMP contains the following components: • Two 500mg caplets of acetaminophen (total 1,000mg) in extended-release form. • One 400mg tablet of moxifloxacin. • One 15mg tablet of meloxicam.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: Each of the three medications in these dosages is contained in a blister pack. Note. The popular nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin interfere with platelet function and blood clotting and can significantly increase the risk of bleeding in combat casualties.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: Acetaminophen and meloxicam do not alter platelet function and are safe and effective for use in combat casualties. Meloxicam does not alter platelet function and is the preferred Non-Steroidal AntiInflammatory Drug for personnel who may see combat in the next 7-10 days.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: The CWMP should be given when the casualty: • Is conscious and able to swallow. • It has mild to moderate pain. • Is still able to fight if needed. • Has any penetrating wounds or break of the skin.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: The CWMP should NOT be given if the casualty: • Is unable to swallow or take oral meds, such as when the casualty is unconscious, or has severe facial trauma, or burns. • Has known allergies to the CWMP medications. • If the casualty is unconscious, refer them to medical personnel as soon as possible. Note. If the casualty has a break in the skin in a traumatic injury, they should take the CWMP. Otherwise, consult with medical personnel before giving it.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: Battlefield wounds are often dirty and susceptible to infection. Early administration of antibiotics from the CWMP may reduce the chance of later infections. Wound infections can kill the casualty or delay their recovery. The CWMP should be given as soon as possible for wounds after life-threatening issues have been addressed.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: Beyond MARCH, there are additional or secondary injuries that should be identified and may need treatment. The secondary injuries identified in TCCC are organized by eye trauma, head injury, burns, and fractures. These secondary injuries are treated in TFC.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: Wound management is the "W" in the MARCH-PAWS sequence. Once the casualty's hemorrhage has been controlled, earlier control interventions are completed, and wound management must be rechecked. All wounds must be frequently reassessed to ensure continued hemorrhage control.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: The first responder or CLS should confirm all wounds have been addressed and reassess for re-bleeding under gauze or bandages to ensure bleeding has been controlled. The first responder or CLS must look for blood flowing around or under TQs, bandages, and dressings. If the bleeding has not been controlled, tighten the TQ or pressure bandage for that wound if possible, and redress any wounds as necessary. Also, check other wounds to make sure that: • Eye injuries are shielded. • Open chest wounds are accounted for. • All wounds are wrapped. • Fractures are splinted.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: Wounds should always be monitored and frequently reassessed to ensure hemorrhage has been controlled. Any wounds that continue to bleed must be packed with new hemostatic dressing. Once the dressing has been applied with pressure for three minutes, carefully observe for blood continuing to flow 94 Secondary Injury Assessment Using Pain, Antibiotics, Wounds, Splinting and Mechanism of Injury, Injury Type, Signs and Symptoms, and Treatments from under the gauze to determine if bleeding has been controlled. When the bleeding has stopped, a new pressure bandage should be applied over the hemostatic dressing.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: Any previously untreated wounds should be dressed by applying (or packing) gauze with direct pressure. Non-life-threatening bleeding usually does not need hemostatic dressing. If dressings or gauze are not available, use clean, dry cloth such as torn clothing, or a cravat if available.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: Minor wounds include minor lacerations and abrasions, such as road rashes. Other wounds that may need to be dressed include major wounds that are no longer bleeding, such as: • Amputation stumps. • Gunshot wounds that required a TQ. • Major lacerations. • Shrapnel wounds, possibly with shrapnel still in place. • Impaled objects.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: Applied pressure bandages must be continuously reassessed for: • Increased pain. • Skin color. • Loss of the pulse.

sections.chapter: Secondary injury assessment using pain, antibiotics,
sections.text: If any of the above develops, it might indicate an emergency. Ensure that the applied bandage isn't too tight and loosen it as needed while keeping the bleeding controlled. Note. Pulses are reassessed after dressings are placed to ensure that they are not too tight. Do not ever apply a dressing and forget it! 95 This page intentionally left blank.

The eye is a vital sensory organ, and blindness is a severe physical handicap. Timely first aid for eye injuries may relieve pain and may help prevent shock, permanent eye injury, and possible loss of vision. The eye is very sensitive: any injury can be easily aggravated if it is improperly handled. Injuries in the eye may be quite severe. Cuts of the eyelids can appear to be very serious, but if the eyeball is not involved, a person's vision usually will not be damaged. However, lacerations (cuts) of the eyeball can cause permanent damage or loss of sight.

Exposure to intense light can burn an individual. Infrared rays, eclipse light (if the casualty has looked directly at the sun), or laser burns cause injuries of the exposed eyeball. Ultraviolet (UV) rays from arc welding can cause a superficial burn to the surface of the eye. These injuries are generally not painful but may cause permanent damage to the eyes. Immediate first aid is usually not required. Loosely bandaging the eyes may make the casualty more comfortable and protect their eyes from further injury caused by exposure to other bright lights or sunlight. Eyesight is one of our most important senses. Damage to an eye can be irreversible if not treated correctly and as early as possible. The following signs should make you suspect a penetrating eye injury: • Bleeding surrounding the eye, inside the eyeball, or coming from the eyeball. • Obvious penetration of shrapnel or debris into the eyeball or eye socket. • Protruding objects from the globe of the eyeball. • Swelling or lacerations of the globe of the eyeball. • Protrusion of the globe of the eyeball from the eye socket. • Reduced vision and swelling of the eye area. • Misshapen or distorted parts of the eye from normal.

sections.section: Equipment used for the treatment of eye trauma
sections.text: The rigid eye shield is a barrier to environmental hazards and to protect the eye by providing a safe enclosure, until additional medical attention is available. The rigid eye shield is normally plastic or metallic, with a domed shape to enhance the protection of eye injuries, without applying pressure. It may be selfadhering or require tape. If a rigid eye shield is not available, or already used, the following may be used as an improvised or expedient rigid eye shield: • Protective glasses. • Clean cup. • Dip can.

sections.section: Equipment used for the treatment of eye trauma
sections.text: The Military Acute Concussion Evaluation 2 Card is an acute assessment tool for all medically trained personnel who treat Service members involved in a potentially concussive event. The Military Acute Concussion Evaluation 2 incorporates current state-of-the-science traumatic brain injury information, which looks at the systems in charge of integrating balance, vision, and movement.

sections.section: TIER 1 SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
sections.text: If a penetrating eye injury is seen or suspected, the first responder must shield the injured eye. The casualties injured eye must be covered with a rigid eye shield, not a pressure patch. In typical situations, a concave shield is placed over the injured eye, (not both eyes), and taped in place. If there is a protruding object in the eye, bandage in place — do not remove the object. Do not waste critical time by conducting further treatment. The casualty should be evacuated as soon as possible. 97

The rigid eye shield is secured over the injured eye with tape at a 45-degree angle across the forehead and cheek. Rigid eye shields should be placed over both eyes only when you are sure and at least suspect that both eyes have been injured. If a rigid eye shield is not available, tactical eyewear may be used to protect the eyes from further trauma.

When only one eye has been injured, do not place a shield over the uninjured eye to prevent eye movement. Movement has not been shown to worsen the outcome for the injured eye. Blindness, resulting from placing eye shields over both eyes unnecessarily, makes an otherwise ambulatory casualty a litter casualty, and is psychologically stressful. The first responder should be prepared to render first aid for lacerations of the eyelid, foreign bodies in the eye, extrusions of the eye, and chemical burns of the eye. INITIATE FIRST AID FOR LACERATIONS OF THE EYELID OR EYEBALL WITH EYE-SHIELD 104B

Lacerated or torn eyelids may bleed heavily, but bleeding usually stops quickly. Cover the injured eye with a sterile dressing. DO NOT put pressure on the wound because you may injure the eyeball. Handle torn eyelids very carefully to prevent further injury. Place any detached pieces of the eyelid on a clean bandage or dressing and immediately send them with the casualty to the medical facility.
Lacerations or cuts to the eyeball may cause serious and permanent eye damage. Cover the injury with a loose sterile dressing. DO NOT put pressure on the eyeball because additional damage may occur.
Survey the situation; if the injury is from chemical exposure, immediately wash the eye. Otherwise, DO NOT put anything on the eye ITSELF, especially if you think the eye is cut.

If necessary, remove the casualty's headgear. Position and treat the casualty as follows: • The conscious casualty will be placed in a seated position. • The unconscious casualty will be placed in a supine position with their head slightly elevated. • Gently clean any dirt or blood from the affected area around the eye.

Examine the eyes for the following: • Objects protruding from the eyes. • Look for foreign objects in or on the eyes and damage to the eyes. • Swelling or lacerations of the eyes. • Bloodshot appearance of the white of the eyes. • Bleeding— ▪ Surrounding the eye. 98 Eye Trauma ▪ ▪ From inside the eyeball. Coming from the eyeball.

Ask the casualty if they are wearing contact lenses, but DO NOT force the eyelids open. Record and communicate to medical personnel (first responders, emergency medical technicians, or combat medics) that contact lenses are being worn.

Categorize the injury as follows: • Injury to the tissue surrounding the eye (lacerations and contusions). • Injury to the eyeball. • Extrusion (the eye is protruding out of the eye socket). • Foreign bodies. • Protruding (impaled) objects. Note. Torn eyelids should be handled carefully. Wrap any fragments in a separate moist dressing and evacuate with the casualty.
Provide first aid for the injury as follows: • Control bleeding with light pressure from a dressing.
Preserve any avulsed (detached) skin or tissue in a clean sterile gauze soaked in saline (if available) and transport it with the casualty for possible grafting.

While seeking CASEVAC or MEDEVAC: • Do not cause further injury. • Limit movements that could cause further injury to the eye. • Do not administer medication to prevent coughing, sneezing, or vomiting.
Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea.

Record first aid administered on the DD Form 1380. Evacuate the casualty: • On their back, with the head elevated and immobilized. • With their corrective eyeglasses, even if they are broken. • Ensure the casualty's personal belongings, such as identification and any critical medications, accompany them during evacuation.

Do not cause further injury to the eye or casualty while waiting for evacuation. Provide assurance to the casualty and stay with the casualty until relieved by medical personnel or competent authority. INITIATE FIRST AID FOR FOREIGN BODIES IN THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD 105B

With impaled objects or significant sized foreign bodies, both eyes are usually bandaged to help secure the foreign body in the injured eye. In a battlefield environment, leave the uninjured eye uncovered so that the casualty can see.

Survey the situation, if the injury is from chemical exposure, immediately wash the eye. Otherwise, DO NOT put anything on the eye ITSELF, especially if you think the eye is cut. Examine the eyes as follows: • Look at the eyes — are the pupils equal and round? 100 Eye Trauma • Look for bleeding or foreign bodies in the eye.

Use the rigid eye-shield provided in the first aid kit, or anything that provides a hard cover over the eye, such as— • Eye protective gear, ballistic glasses, or goggles. • The bottom of a disposable cup, for example one made of extruded polystyrene (foam), plastic, or paper. Note. This helps prevent any undue pressure or further damage to the eye. DO NOT put any pressure on the eye. • Secure the rigid eye-shield by applying tape from the cheek to the forehead. If tape is unavailable, use gauze, cloth dressing, shoelace, or string to secure in place.

Apply dry sterile dressings to build around and support the object. This will help prevent further contamination and minimize movement of the object. Cover the injured eye with a paper cup or cardboard cone.

Obtain details about the injury— • Source and type of foreign bodies if known. • Whether the foreign bodies were windblown, or by what type of high-velocity mechanism. • Time of onset and length of discomfort. • Any previous injuries to the eye.

Do not cause additional injury to the eye— • Do not probe for foreign bodies. • Do not put pressure on the eyeball. • Do not remove the impaled object. 101 • • Limit movements that could cause further eye injury. Do not administer medication to prevent coughing, sneezing, or vomiting.
Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury, and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea.
Record the first aid administered and other information as required on the DD Form 1380 (provided in the first aid kit).

Do not cause further injury to the eye or casualty while waiting for evacuation. Provide assurance and stay with the casualty until relieved by medical personnel or competent authority. INITIATE FIRST AID FOR EXTRUSIONS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD 106B

Service members may encounter casualties with severe eye injuries that include an extruded eyeball (eyeball out-of-socket). In such instances, you should gently cover the extruded eye with a loose moistened dressing and cover the unaffected eye. DO NOT bind or exert pressure on the injured eye while applying the dressing. Keep the casualty quiet, place them on their back, treat for shock, and evacuate them immediately.

Position a— • Conscious casualty in a seated position. • Reassure and inform the conscious casualty of the first aid steps that you are providing. • Unconscious casualty lying on their back with their head slightly elevated.

Examine the eyes for— • Objects protruding from the eye or eyes. • Swelling or lacerations of the eyes. • Bloodshot appearance of the eyes. • Bleeding— ▪ Surrounding the eye. ▪ From inside the eyeball. ▪ Coming from the eyeball. • Contact lenses. Ask the casualty if they are wearing contact lenses, however, do not force the eyelids open. • Extrusion (the eye is protruding from the socket).

Provide appropriate first aid for the injury as follows: • Position the casualty face up. • Cut a hole into several layers of dressing material and then moisten it. Use sterile or the cleanest water if available, preferably potable. 102 Eye Trauma • Gently place the dressing so the injured eyeball protrudes through the hole, with minimal contact. Surround and protect the eyeball, minimizing the movement of the dressing. The dressing should be built up higher than the eyeball. Note. If available, place a paper cup or cone-shaped piece of cardboard over the eye. This material should not touch the eye. Do not apply pressure to the injury site. Apply roller gauze to hold the cup in place. • The provided rigid eye-shield will not be deep enough to properly protect the eye extrusion injury.
Call for medical aid immediately and arrange for MEDEVAC as soon as possible.

While calling for CASEVAC or MEDEVAC — • Limit movements that could cause further eye injury. • Do not administer medication to prevent coughing, sneezing, or vomiting. • Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury, and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea.

Record first aid administered on the DD Form 1380. Evacuate the casualty: • On their back, with the head elevated and immobilized. • With their corrective eyeglasses, even if they are broken. • Ensure the casualty's personal belongings, such as identification and any critical medications, accompany them during evacuation.

Do not cause further injury to the eye or casualty while waiting for evacuation. Provide assurance and stay with the casualty until relieved by medical personnel or competent authority. INITIATE FIRST AID FOR CHEMICAL BURNS OF THE EYE WITH AN EYE-SHIELD 107B

Injuries from chemical burns require immediate first aid. Mainly acids or alkalis cause chemical burns. The first aid measures consist of flushing the eyes immediately with large amounts of water for at least 5 to 20 minutes, or as long as necessary to flush out the chemical and, once flushed, bandaging the eyes. If the burn is an acid burn, you should flush the eye for at least 5 to 10 minutes. If the burn is an alkali burn, you should flush the eye for at least 20 minutes. After the eye has been flushed, evacuate the casualty immediately.

When an individual suffers burns of the face from a fire, the eyes will close quickly due to extreme heat. This reaction is a natural reflex to protect the eyeballs; however, the eyelids remain exposed to possibly being burned. If a casualty receives burns of the eyelids or face— • DO NOT apply dressing. • DO NOT touch. • SEEK medical assistance immediately.

Quickly identify the substance that the casualty was exposed to such as— Note. Do not delay first aid to perform this step. Time is critical and the eyes must be irrigated as soon as possible. • Alkali substances, which are the most dangerous of all substances are due to the penetrating factor. Common substances that contain the hydroxides of ammonia, lye, potassium, magnesium, and lime are— 103 • • ▪ Fertilizers. ▪ Cleaning products such as drain cleaners, and oven cleaners. ▪ Plaster and cement. Acid substances are usually less severe than alkali burns. Common acids contain sulfuric, hydrochloric, nitric, acetic, chromic, and hydrofluoric acids are— ▪ Glass polish, vinegar, and nail polish remover. ▪ Automobile battery acid. Irritants and substances that have a neutral power of hydrogen tend to cause more discomfort to the eye. Examples of irritants that may cause this damage are— ▪ Most household detergents. ▪ Pepper spray. ▪ Smoke from burning chemicals or rubber.

Check for the following signs and symptoms: • Irritation. • Pain and redness. • Watering and tearing. • Possible erosion of the corneal surface. • Inability to keep the eye open. • Swelling of the eyelid. • Blurred vision.

Initiate first aid for the chemical burn as follows: • IMMEDIATELY flood the eye with water. • Keep irrigating the eye with running water from a faucet, low-pressure hose, bottle, cup, or intravenous setup (if available). • Hold the irrigating tip 1 to 1½ inches away from the casualty's eye or eyes, direct the irrigating solution gently from the inner eye (nearest the nose) to the outer eye (towards the ear) from the casualty's unaffected eye. • Start the transport and continue washing out the eye or eyes for at least 20 minutes or until the casualty's arrival at the MTF. • Dry the area around the eye or eyes by gently patting with gauze sponges or other appropriate clean material. Do not touch the casualty's eye. • Cover the injured eye or eyes with the rigid eye-shield provided in the first aid kit, or an appropriate device that provides a hard cover over the eye such as: ▪ Eye protective gear, ballistic glasses, or goggles. ▪ The bottom of a disposable cup made of extruded polystyrene (foam), plastic, or paper. • Secure the rigid eye-shield by applying tape from the cheek to the forehead. If tape is unavailable, use gauze, cloth dressing, shoelace, or string to secure in place. Note 1. In hostile environments (such as combat or unsure footing), the eyes may have to remain uncovered so the casualty can see getting away from danger. Note 2. Burned eyelids swell to protect the underlying eyes. The eyes should be protected with the rigid eye-shield to prevent further injury. 104 Eye Trauma
Do not cause further injury to the eye by limiting movement that could cause further eye injury. Do not administer medication that prevents coughing, sneezing, or vomiting.
Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury, and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea.
Record the first aid given on the DD Form 1380 (provided in the first aid kit).

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
sections.text: If a penetrating eye injury is noted or suspected, four steps must be taken: • Perform a rapid field test of visual acuity. Rapid visual acuity testing includes: ▪ Read print. ▪ Count fingers. ▪ Identity hand motion. ▪ Sense light perception. • Cover the affected eye with a rigid eye shield, NOT a pressure patch. A pressure dressing could result in permanent loss of vision. Place a rigid eye shield on only one eye, unless both eyes are injured. Covering both eyes turns an otherwise ambulatory casualty into a litter casualty. Tactical eyewear is always a good way to prevent eye issues and can be used for protection if no eye shield is available. • Administer the casualty's complete CWMP, including all the medications contained in it. One of the medications is 400mg of moxifloxacin, which can be administered to prevent infection. • Document all findings and treatments on the casualty's DD Form 1380.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS USED TO TREAT EYE TRAUMA
sections.text: Pressure on the eye could force the interior contents of the eye out of the eyeball through a cut or laceration. For protruding or impaled objects extending past the eye shield, cut a hole in the eye shield to allow the object to fit through, and secure it in place. If the eye shield cannot be applied around the impaled object, then use an improvised eye shield to avoid pressure on the eye.

sections.section: Expedient skills used to treat eye trauma
sections.text: There are several expedient skills that can be employed to provide immediate care for eye trauma. Eye trauma should always be evaluated and treated by a qualified medical professional as soon as possible. The following are some skills or techniques that may be used in the initial management of eye trauma: • Protecting the eye: If there is a foreign object, such as debris or a penetrating object, near or embedded in the eye, it's crucial to prevent further injury. Avoid touching or rubbing the eye, as this can exacerbate the damage. Place a protective shield or cup over the eye, if available, to prevent accidental contact. • Flushing the eye: If there are chemicals or irritants in the eye, use immediate and gentle irrigation with clean water, or saline solution can help flush out the substance. Tilt the head to the side and pour a gentle stream of fluid over the eye from the inner corner to the outer corner. Use a clean container or a commercially available eye wash bottle. • Covering injuries: If there is a cut or laceration around the eye, apply a sterile dressing or clean cloth to cover the wound. Avoid applying pressure directly on the eye. Secure the dressing in place with a bandage or adhesive tape. 105 • • Immobilizing the eye: If there is a suspected or evident fracture of the eye socket or orbit, it may be necessary to immobilize the eye to prevent further injury. Place a protective shield or a cup over the eye and use a bandage or tape to secure it in position. This can help stabilize the injured area until medical attention is available. Applying cold compresses:

sections.section: Expedient skills used to treat eye trauma
sections.text: The above expedient skills are meant to provide initial first aid and should not replace professional medical care. The casualty should be evacuated as soon as possible to supporting MTF to ensure a thorough evaluation and appropriate treatment for eye trauma. 106

Head injuries are a common concern that can occur due to accidents, falls, or sports-related incidents. When the head experiences a forceful impact, it can result in different types of injuries. Understanding head injuries can help Service members take the necessary precautions to protect themselves or others from potential harm. It is critically important to report findings of a head injury to medical personnel at the scene since a lack of rapid, and appropriate medical care can worsen the head injury, and the eventual outcome. Head trauma can be either blunt or penetrating. Head injuries can be broadly classified as open or closed head injuries.

An open head injury, also known as an open skull injury, is a type of injury that occurs when there is a break or penetration of the skull, exposing the brain to the external environment. It typically involves visible damage to the scalp, skull, or meninges (protective coverings of the brain). The signs and symptoms of an open head injury can vary depending on the severity and specific location of the injury. Open head injuries are considered medical emergencies. If an open head injury is suspected, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention for evaluation, diagnosis, and appropriate treatment.

The common signs and symptoms associated with an open head injury are: • Visible head wound. An open head injury often involves a visible wound or laceration on the scalp or skull. There may be bleeding, or an open fracture where the bone is exposed. • Profuse bleeding. Open head injuries can cause significant bleeding due to damage to blood vessels. Blood may be visible on the scalp, face, or in severe cases, there may be profuse bleeding from the head wound. • Skull deformity. In some cases, an open head injury may cause a visible deformity or depression in the skull, indicating a skull fracture or bone displacement. • Loss of consciousness. Depending on the severity of the injury, loss of consciousness can occur, ranging from a brief period to an extended duration. • Clear fluid or blood drainage. Leakage of clear fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) or blood from the nose, ears, or wound can indicate a more severe injury and should be treated as an emergency. • Severe headache. An intense and persistent headache is common following an open head injury. • Nausea and vomiting. Feelings of nausea and vomiting may be present after an open head injury. • Confusion and disorientation. The Service member may exhibit confusion, memory loss, difficulty concentrating, or may appear disoriented. • Seizures. Seizures can occur after an open head injury, especially if the brain is directly affected. • Changes in speech or vision. The person may have difficulties with speech, vision problems, double vision, or other sensory disturbances. • Weaknesses or numbness. Weakness or numbness in certa

A closed head injury refers to trauma to the head that does not involve an open wound or penetration of the skull. Instead, the injury occurs internally, within the skull. Closed head injuries are often the result of blunt force impacts, falls, or accidents, where the brain is subjected to sudden acceleration, deceleration, or rotational forces. Concussions are the most common type of a closed head injury. Closed head injuries may not be obvious or detectable.

Closed head injuries can range in severity from mild concussions to more severe forms, such as contusions, diffuse axonal injuries, or intracranial hemorrhages. It is essential to seek medical attention if a 107 closed head injury is suspected, as the impact on the brain can have serious consequences and requires appropriate evaluation and management.

The signs and symptoms of a closed head injury can vary depending on the severity of the injury. Mild cases may be present with subtle symptoms, while more severe injuries can have immediate and pronounced effects. The common signs and symptoms associated with a closed head injury are: • Headache or pressure in the head. • Nausea and vomiting. • Dizziness and balance problems. • Confusion and disorientation. • Memory loss or difficulty concentrating. • Mood and behavior changes. • Sensory changes, such as blurred vision, or ringing in the ears. • Sensitivity to light and sound. • Loss of consciousness (in severe cases).

It is important to seek medical attention if any of these signs are present after a head injury, as they can indicate a range of severity from a mild concussion to more serious brain trauma. The above symptoms can occur immediately after the injury or may develop gradually over time. Symptoms may vary from person to person.

A concussion is a type of traumatic brain injury that occurs when the brain experiences a sudden and forceful movement within the skull. It is typically caused by a blow, jolt, or bump to the head or body, which can disrupt the normal functioning of the brain.

Concussions can occur in various situations, such as sports-related injuries, falls, motor vehicle accidents, or any other incident involving a significant impact to the head. Concussions can happen even without a direct impact to the head. The forceful movement or shaking of the body can still cause the brain to move inside the skull, leading to a concussion.

The primary characteristic of a concussion is a temporary disruption of brain function. Concussions may not always involve a loss of consciousness. In fact, most concussions occur without a person losing consciousness. Common symptoms of a concussion can include: • Headache or pressure in the head. • Dizziness or feeling lightheaded. • Confusion or feeling mentally foggy. • Memory problems or difficulty concentrating. • Fatigue or feeling tired. • Nausea or vomiting. • Sensitivity to light or noise. • Changes in sleep patterns. • Irritability or changes in mood. • Blurred vision or difficulty with balance.

It's important to seek medical attention if a concussion is suspected, as health care professionals can evaluate the severity of the injury and provide appropriate guidance for recovery. The initial management of a concussion involves rest and avoiding activities that could further injure the brain. Physical and cognitive rest are recommended to allow the brain to heal properly. In some cases, individuals may need to temporarily limit activities like school or work to promote recovery. A gradual return to normal activities is typically recommended under the guidance of a health care professional.

Every concussion is unique, and the symptoms and recovery time can vary from person to person. With proper rest, most individuals recover fully from a concussion. However, in some cases, symptoms may persist or worsen, and a condition known as post-concussion syndrome may develop. 108 Head Injury

A contusion refers to a type of injury characterized by damage to the tissue or blood vessels beneath the skin, usually resulting from a blunt force impact. It is commonly known as a bruise. When a contusion occurs, blood vessels are damaged, leading to bleeding and the subsequent discoloration of the skin.

In relation to head injuries, contusions can occur because of a direct blow or trauma to the head. When the head experiences a significant impact, the brain can collide with the inner surface of the skull, leading to contusions. These types of injuries are known as cerebral contusions.

Cerebral contusions can be classified as coup-contrecoup injuries, which means that contusions can occur both at the site of impact (coup) and on the opposite side of the brain due to the brain rebounding and hitting the skull (contrecoup). These injuries are concerning because they involve damage to the brain tissue itself.

The severity of a cerebral contusion can vary, ranging from mild to severe. In more severe cases, contusions can lead to increased pressure within the skull, swelling of the brain, and potentially lifethreatening complications.

It is crucial to seek immediate medical attention if a head injury is suspected, as prompt evaluation and treatment are essential to prevent further complications. Symptoms of a cerebral contusion may include: • Changes in vision. • Confusion. • Difficulty speaking. • Dizziness. • Headache. • Loss of consciousness. • Nausea. • Seizures. • Vomiting. • Weaknesses.

Treatment for cerebral contusions focuses on managing the underlying injury and preventing further damage. It may involve measures such as rest, pain management, observation, close monitoring of neurological status, and, in more severe cases, surgical intervention to relieve pressure and remove any blood clots or damaged tissue.

sections.section: Equipment used for the treatment of a head injury
sections.text: Treating a head wound requires few essential pieces of equipment. Service members will need disposable gloves to protect themselves and the injured person from any potential infection. Sterile gauze pads or clean clothes are vital for covering and applying pressure to the wound to stop the bleeding. Adhesive bandages or medical tape are used to secure the gauze in place. Additionally, a mild antiseptic solution or wipes are important for cleaning the wound to prevent infection. Lastly, a cravat or gauze bandage can be used to create a makeshift dressing or sling to support the head if there is a suspected skull or neck injury.

sections.section: TIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
sections.text: Service members may not have the time or expertise to conduct extensive treatment for a head injury. Service members experiencing any of the symptoms explained in paragraph 11-17 should be evacuated as soon as tactically feasible.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
sections.text: Service members experiencing any of the symptoms explained in paragraph 11-17 should be evacuated as soon as tactically feasible. However, the CLS should complete the injury/evaluation/distance (commonly known as I.E.D.) checklist that is outlined in DODI 6490.11. This checklist is used to gather information, and to identify the signs and symptoms of a head injury. 109

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF A HEAD INJURY
sections.text: Commanders or their representatives are required to assess all Service members involved in potentially concussive events, including those without apparent injuries, as soon as possible using the injury/evaluation/distance checklist (figure 11-1).

Service members who are involved in a potentially concussive event, as specified in DODI 6490.11, must be referred for a medical evaluation. This referral is mandatory if they answer "Yes" on the injury/evaluation/distance checklist or exhibit any symptoms associated with concussion at any point following the incident. Once the injury/evaluation/distance assessment is concluded, it is crucial to document the results for all individuals involved in the event. These records should then be submitted as part of the significant activities report, which is required for all blast-related incidents or other events outlined in DODI 6490.11. This procedure ensures that all potential concussions are promptly and effectively addressed, safeguarding the health and well-being of the Service members.

When dealing with trauma casualties suspected of having a head injury, it is crucial to report specific critical observations to medical personnel in accordance with the Military Acute Concussive Evaluation 2 (known as MACE 2). Immediate evaluation following the injury significantly enhances the effectiveness of the assessments. A traumatic brain injury should be suspected if the casualty exhibits any of the following signs: • A deteriorating level of consciousness. • Experiencing double vision. • Exhibiting increased restlessness, combative, or agitated behavior. • Repeated vomiting. • Positive results from a structural brain injury detection device, if available. • Seizures. • Weakness or tingling sensations in the arms or legs. • Severe or worsening headache.

If any of these signs or symptoms are present, they must be reported immediately to the arriving medical personnel. For comprehensive guidelines on reporting and treating head injuries, refer to DODI 6490.11. This protocol ensures that potential traumatic brain injuries are promptly identified and appropriately managed.

Some wounds and burns will require special precautions and procedures when applying these measures. This section discusses specific first aid procedures for wounds of the head, neck, and facial injuries. It also discusses the techniques for applying dressings and bandages to specific parts of the body.

Head injuries range from minor abrasions or cuts on the scalp, to severe brain injuries that may result in unconsciousness and sometimes death. Head injuries are classified as open or closed wounds. An open wound is one that is visible, has a break in the skin, and usually has evidence of bleeding. A closed wound may be visible (such as a depression in the skull) or the first aid provider may not be able to see an apparent injury (such as internal bleeding). Some head injuries result in unconsciousness; however, a Service member may have a serious head wound and still be conscious. Casualties with blunt trauma should be treated as though they also have a spinal injury. The casualty should not be moved until the head and neck are stabilized unless they are in immediate danger (such as close to a burning vehicle). 110 Head Injury

Prompt first aid measures should be initiated for casualties with suspected head and neck injuries. The conscious casualty may be able to provide information on the extent of their injuries. However, because of the head injury, they may be confused and unable to provide accurate information. The signs and symptoms that a first aid provider might observe are: • Nausea and vomiting. • Convulsions or twitches. • Slurred speech. • Confusion and loss of memory. (Do they know who they are? Do they know where they are? Do they know what day it is?). • Recent unconsciousness. • Dizziness. • Drowsiness. • Blurred vision, unequal pupils, or bruising (black eyes). • Paralysis (partial or full). • Complaint of headache. • Bleeding or other fluid discharge from the scalp, nose, or ears. • Deformity of the head (depression or swelling). • Staggering while walking.

When encountering an unconscious casualty, it is essential to act swiftly and methodically, as their condition may be critical. Unconsciousness can result from various causes, such as trauma, medical emergencies, or underlying health conditions. The primary objective of first aid for an unconscious patient is to ensure their immediate safety, preserve their airway, and seek professional medical help. By following specific guidelines and employing basic life support techniques, first responders can play a vital role in providing initial assistance until medical professionals arrive. An unconscious casualty does not have control of all their functions and may choke on their tongue, blood, vomitus, or other substances resulting in: • Loss of Breathing. The brain requires a constant supply of oxygen. A bluish (or an individual with dark skin-grayish) color of skin around the lips and nail beds indicates that the casualty is not receiving enough oxygen. Immediate action must be taken to clear the airway, to position the casualty on their side, or to initiate rescue breathing. • Bleeding. Bleeding from a head injury usually comes from blood vessels within the scalp. Bleeding can also develop inside the skull or within the brain. In most instances visible bleeding from the head can be controlled by application of the field first aid dressing.

Provide direct manual stabilization of the head by placing your hands on each side of the casualty's head, maintaining the position of the head in line with the body. Assess the casualty's level of consciousness utilizing the alert, verbal, pain, and unresponsive (AVPU) method. AVPU is determined by asking— • Is the casualty alert? A. • Does the casualty respond to verbal stimuli or commands? V. • Does the casualty respond to painful stimulus? P. • Is the casualty unconscious? U.

The casualty with a head injury (or suspected head injury) should be continually monitored for the development of conditions that may require basic lifesaving measures. After initiating first aid measures, request medical assistance and evacuation. If dedicated MEDEVAC assets are not available, transport the casualty to an MTF as soon as the situation permits. The first aid provider should not attempt to remove a protruding object from the head or give the casualty anything to eat or drink. Furthermore, the first aid provider should be prepared to— • Clear the airway. • Control bleeding (external). • Administer first aid measures for shock. • Keep the casualty warm. • Protect the wound.

sections.section: Initiate Treatment for a Superficial Head Injury
sections.text: Provide first aid for a superficial head injury by— • Applying a dressing. • Observing for abnormal behavior or evidence of complications. • Documenting on the TCCC card.

Provide first aid for a head injury involving trauma as follows: • Maintain a patent airway using the jaw-thrust maneuver. • Dress the head wounds. • Control bleeding. • Treat for shock. • Seek medical aid. • Monitor the casualty for convulsions or seizures.

Monitor unstable casualties for the following— • Level of consciousness by using the AVPU indicators. • Pupils respond to light and are equal in size. • Motor functions, casualty's strength, mobility, coordination, and sensation. 112 Head Injury • • Seek medical aid. Evacuate the casualty as soon as possible.

Neck injuries may result in heavy bleeding. Apply pressure above and below the injury. Do not interfere with the breathing process and attempt to control the bleeding. Apply a dressing. When blunt trauma occurs, always evaluate the casualty for a possible neck fracture or spinal cord injury; if suspected, seek medical treatment immediately. Note. Establish and maintain the airway in cases of facial or neck injuries. If a neck fracture or spinal cord injury is suspected, immobilize the injury and, if necessary, perform basic life support measures.

Soft tissue injuries of the face and scalp are common. Abrasions (scrapes) of the skin do not cause serious problems. Contusions (injury without a break in the skin) usually cause swelling. A contusion of the scalp looks and feels like a lump. Laceration (cut) and avulsion (torn away tissue) injuries are common. Avulsions are frequently caused when a sharp blow separates the scalp from the skull beneath it. The face and scalp are richly supplied with blood vessels (arteries and veins) and the wounds of these areas usually bleed heavily.

Lacerated (cut) or avulsed (torn) ear tissue may not be a serious injury. Bleeding, or the drainage of fluids from the ear canal, however, may be a sign of a head injury, such as a skull fracture. DO NOT attempt to stop the flow from the inner ear canal or put anything into the ear canal to block it. Instead, you should cover the ear lightly with a dressing. For minor cuts or wounds to the external ear, apply a cravat or gauze bandage as follows: • Place the middle of the bandage over the ear (figure 11-2 step A). • Cross the ends, wrap them in opposite directions around the head, and tie them (figure 11-2 step B and figure 11-2 step C). • If possible, place some dressing material between the back of the ear and the side of the head to avoid crushing the ear against the head with the bandage.

Nose injuries generally produce bleeding. The bleeding may be controlled by placing an ice pack (if available) over the nose or pinching the nostrils together. The bleeding may also be controlled by placing torn gauze (rolled) between the upper teeth and the lip. 113

Before applying a bandage to a casualty's jaw, remove all loose or free-floating foreign material from the casualty's mouth. If the casualty is unconscious, check for obstructions in the airway and remove if possible. If there is profuse bleeding in the oral cavity, the cavity may require loose packing with soft bandaging material prior to applying a bandage. Care should be taken to avoid occluding the airway.

When applying the bandage, allow the jaw enough freedom to permit passage of air and drainage from the mouth. Dress the wound, and apply the bandages by— • Placing the bandage under the chin and pull its ends upward. Adjust the bandage to make one end longer than the other (figure 11-3 step A). • Taking the longer end over the top of the head to meet the short end at the temple and cross the ends over (figure 11-3 step B). • Wrapping the ends in opposite directions to the other side of the head and tying them over the part of the bandage that was applied first (figure 11-3 step C). Note. The bandaging procedure outlined is the cravat technique used to immobilize a fractured jaw 114

A burned trauma casualty should be treated for all other life-threatening injuries first, following the MARCH-PAWS sequence, before addressing burns. Even if the skin is burned, trauma treatments can still be performed on or through it.

Burns can result from various causes: • Friction Burns. These are common in situations where skin is rubbed off against a hard surface, often seen in road accidents where motorcycle riders, cyclists, or skateboarders slide across pavement, getting what's known as "road rash." Carpet burns occur from skin scraping against carpet, often during indoor sports or play. Rope burns are common during activities like climbing or tug-of-war, and sliding burns frequently happen in sports like baseball when sliding into bases. • Cold Burns. Also known as frostbite, these burns damage the skin by freezing it. Frostbite can occur from prolonged exposure to freezing temperatures or direct contact with extremely cold objects. • Thermal Burns. These occur when the skin touches something very hot, like hot metals, scalding liquids, flames, or steam, raising the skin temperature high enough to kill skin cells. • Radiation Burns. Sunburn is a typical example. Other sources include X-rays or radiation therapy for cancer. • Chemical Burns. These happen when strong acids, solvents, or detergents come into contact with the skin. • Electrical Burns. These burns are the result of contact with electrical currents.

Burns are classified based on how deeply they damage the skin: • Superficial or First Degree Burns (figure 12-1 on page 116): Superficial burns affect only the outer layer of the skin, causing redness, pain, and mild swelling. They are like mild sunburn and usually heal within a few days without leaving scars. • Partial thickness or Second Degree Burns (figure 12-2 on page 116): Partial thickness burns reach the second layer of the skin and can cause blisters, severe pain, redness, and swelling. Healing times vary, and these burns may leave scars. • Full thickness or Third Degree Burns (figure 12-3 on page 116): Full thickness burns are the most severe, these burns go through the entire thickness of the skin and can damage muscles or bones underneath. The skin may look white, blackened, or charred, and there might be no feeling in the area because of nerve damage. These burns require immediate medical attention and often need skin grafts to heal. 115 Superficial burn Partial thickness burn Full thickness burn

The size of or percentage of the burn area will be documented on DD Form 1380. The "Rule of Nines" is used to determine or estimate the burn percentage. Figure 12-4 shows the approximation for each area of the body. The body is divided into areas with each having a percentage of the total body surface area as follows: • Head – 9 percent. • Torso (front) – 18 percent. • Torso (back) – 18 percent. • Arms – 9 percent each. • Legs – 18 percent each. • Pubic area – 1 percent. • Buttocks – 1 percent. Note. First degree or superficial burns are not part of the burn percentage calculation and are rarely of medical significance. 116 Burns

General guidelines are that the size of the casualty's palm of the hand represents approximately 1 percent of the burned area. When estimating, it is easiest to round up to the nearest 10 percent. If half of the front or rear area is burned, the area would be half of the area value. For example, if half of the front upper leg or front lower leg were burned, it would be half of 9 percent, or 4.5 percent. If half of the front torso were burned, say either the upper or the lower part of the front torso, then it would be half of 18 percent or 9 percent. Remember, the higher the percentage burned, the higher the chance is for hypothermia.

sections.section: Equipment used for the treatment of burns
sections.text: The CoTCCC-recommended compressed gauze and or gauze rolls are 6-ply sterile cotton that has been compressed. They are used to stop minor bleeding, cover wounds or burns, pack wounds, act as bulky material for pressure dressings, or pad pressure points in splinting.

sections.section: Equipment used for the treatment of burns
sections.text: The CoTCCC-recommended elastic bandage is a stretchable bandage. They are used to hold dressings or splints in place or can be applied more tightly to apply localized pressure on a wound. Elastic or restrictive bandages are normally not applied to a burn casualty. The application of these types of bandages are very painful and swelling secondary to the injury may restrict circulation.

sections.section: Equipment used for the treatment of burns
sections.text: The cravat is a sterile triangular shaped bandage. It can be used as both a bandage and a sling. It is commonly used to secure a splint, create a sling, or swath for an injured limb.

sections.section: TIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
sections.text: Burn care in TCCC is very basic. Eliminating the source of the burn should be the initial priority. Providing any treatment prior to removing the casualty from the source of the burn or extinguishing the cause of the burn will be ineffective and harmful to the casualty and casualty response personnel.

sections.section: TIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
sections.text: Electrical burn care consists of— • Eliminating the source of electrical burns. • Turning off any sources of electricity that have been exposed to the casualty (if applicable). • Using nonconductive material to drag the casualty away from the electrical source (if it cannot be turned off). Note. Types of nonconductive material include rope, clothing, and dry wood. • Moving the casualty to a safe place.

Thermal burn care consists of— • Stopping the source of the thermal burn and remove the casualty from the source of the burn. • Extinguishing any flames on the casualty, cut the clothing around the burned area, and gently lift away.

Chemical burn care consists of— • Eliminating the source of chemical burns. • Brushing off dry chemicals (carefully) with a clean, dry cloth. • Flush the burned area with copious amounts of flowing water to remove any liquid chemicals. • Applying a wet barrier (water-soaked gauze, clothing, or mud) with an occlusive dressing. • Advising medical personnel immediately.

All burn care consists of— • Monitoring the casualty for life-threatening conditions. • Checking for additional injuries. • Treating for shock (if applicable). • Seeking medical aid. • Annotating all treatment and care on DD Form 1380.
Close attention to the casualty's airway, breathing is required and always assess for secondary injuries and shock.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
sections.text: Along with the treatment measures outlined in paragraph 13-9 through 13-14 extra emphasis should be placed on heat loss prevention methods. Burn patients are particularly susceptible to hypothermia. Casualties should be kept off the ground and placed onto an insulated surface as soon as possible.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
sections.text: For extensive burns, those with greater than 20 percent of the area burned place the casualty in the Heat Reflective Shield to cover the burned areas and prevent hypothermia. Preventing and managing hypothermia for burn patients is important and occurs regardless of the ambient temperature in the environment.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
sections.text: Facial burns, especially those that occur in closed spaces, may be associated with an inhalation injury. These casualties should be monitored closely for potential airway issues. Do not place an NPA in a casualty with signs of inhalation burns. Notify medical personnel as soon as possible if an inhalation injury is suspected.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
sections.text: Analgesia may be administered to treat burn pain. Antibiotic therapy is not solely indicated for burns; it should also be given to prevent infection in penetrating wounds. Consider giving the entire combat pill pack if medical treatment takes more than three hours from the time of injury, and if giving the medication to the casualty does not cause nausea.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF BURNS
sections.text: Interventions for warm and cool weather should be considered. The addition of blood loss can cause the body's temperature to drop even when it is hot outside. The TQs should not be covered; keep them visible so medical personnel can easily see it.

sections.section: Expedient skills used for the treatment of burns
sections.text: In emergency scenarios, especially in remote or combat zones, effectively managing burn injuries with limited resources is essential. Basic materials such as gauze bandage, clean clothing, and cravats can be used to cover burns and control bleeding. Cooling and cleaning burns should be done with available clean water, avoiding ice to prevent further skin damage. For thermal burns, it's crucial to remove the casualty from the heat source and cut away clothing gently around the burn area. In cases of electrical burns, disconnecting the power and using non-conductive materials to move the casualty is vital, while chemical burns require immediate decontamination by brushing off dry chemicals and flushing the area thoroughly with water. 118 Burns

sections.section: Expedient skills used for the treatment of burns
sections.text: Preventing hypothermia is critical in burn care due to the high risk posed by skin damage. Using emergency blankets, reflective heat shields, or makeshift insulation from natural materials can help maintain body temperature. Pain management, when possible, should include safe administration of over-the-counter pain relievers, and continuous monitoring for shock is essential. These field expedient techniques are pivotal in stabilizing burn victims and preventing further injury until more advanced medical help can be accessed, underscoring the importance of training and preparedness in these emergency interventions. 119 This page intentionally left blank.

Prompt and appropriate management of fractures, or breaks in bones, is essential to minimize further harm and optimize the chances of survival for injured individuals. TCCC emphasizes a systematic approach to fracture care, incorporating principles such as rapid assessment, stabilization, and pain management. The goal is to provide efficient and effective treatment, considering the challenges of the tactical environment where resources may be limited, and evacuation to definitive care may be delayed. Mastery of fracture management in TCCC equips military personnel and first responders with the skills necessary to stabilize fractures, prevent complications, and facilitate the evacuation process, ultimately improving the overall outcomes for casualties in the field.

The musculoskeletal system provides a structural framework for the body and, because bones are rigid, provides support and protection for vital organs and softer tissues. Skeletal muscles and bones work together to make body movement possible.
The musculoskeletal system is composed of— • Bones. • Joints. • Muscles. • Cartilage. • Ligaments. • Tendons.

Bones are the substance that forms the skeleton of the body. It is composed chiefly of calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate. The human body has 206 bones. There are 80 axial (head and trunk) bones and 126 appendicular (upper and lower extremity) bones. Bones provide structural support for the body. Individual and groups of bones provide structure for the attachment of soft tissues and protect organs.
The human body's mobility hinges on its joints, where bones connect and facilitate movement. These pivotal junctures come in various forms, each serving distinct functions in enabling motion.

The body's muscles serve as its powerhouse, providing the force needed for movement and various physiological functions. Within the body, there exist three main types of muscles, each with its unique roles and characteristics. These include skeletal muscles, which control movement in the extremities and outer body areas, cardiac muscles, found exclusively in the heart, and smooth muscles, lining the walls of arteries and the gastrointestinal tract.

Cartilage serves as a resilient and pliable tissue that provides cushioning and support between bones at the joints, facilitating smooth movement. In addition to its role in joint function, cartilage also forms essential structures elsewhere in the body, such as the larynx and the external portions of the ears, contributing to their flexibility and shape. 121 Ligaments 364B

Ligaments play a crucial role in the body's structural integrity, serving as sturdy bands of connective tissue that link bones together at joints. They provide stability and support, helping to prevent excessive movement and potential joint injuries.

Tendons serve as soft tissue connectors that attach muscles to bones, enabling movement and transmitting the force generated by muscles to the bones they are connected to. Despite their flexibility, tendons possess considerable toughness, providing durability to withstand the stresses of movement and physical activity.

A fracture can be a closed or open fracture. A closed fracture (see figure 13-1) means that there is no external wound associated with the fracture. An open fracture (see figure 13-2) means that there is a break in the skin in conjunction with the fracture, often with protruding bone. The warning signs that an arm or leg might be fractured include: • Significant pain along with marked swelling. • An audible or perceived "snap." • Different length or shape of limb. • Loss of pulse or sensation in the injured arm or leg. • Crepitus (a crackling or popping sound under the skin).

sections.section: Equipment used for the treatment of fractures
sections.text: The CoTCCC endorses the use of the semi-rigid splint, a 36-inch-long malleable device comprised of moldable aluminum, encased in foam padding. This type of splint is designed for versatility in the field and is most commonly employed for stabilizing fractures. Its flexible yet sturdy structure allows it to be shaped according to the specific contours of the injury site, providing effective support and immobilization needed to prevent further injury during transport or until more definitive care can be administered. 122 Fractures and Splinting TIER 1 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF FRACTURES 251B

sections.section: Equipment used for the treatment of fractures
sections.text: During the TFC phase, it is highly advisable to splint all fractures if circumstances permit. Splinting is crucial to immobilize the affected area, preventing further damage, and minimizing pain for the casualty. Proper splinting techniques ensure that fractures are adequately supported until the injured individual receives comprehensive medical treatment. For detailed guidance on how to correctly apply splints, refer to paragraph 14-13, which provides specific instructions and considerations for effective splintering in a tactical environment.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF FRACTURES
sections.text: The "S" in MARCH-PAWS protocol denotes splinting, a crucial step in managing both open and closed fractures. For more information on fractures see paragraph 14-10 on page 122. Splinting involves immobilizing the injured limb to prevent further movement, typically using semi-rigid splints or improvised materials like boards or tree limbs. It's essential to incorporate the joints above and below the fracture site for stability and secure the splint firmly with wraps, belts, or tape. Additionally, securing arm fractures to the shirt using the sleeve as a sling can provide added support. However, caution must be exercised to avoid excessive tightness, which can compromise circulation to the fingers or toes.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF FRACTURES
sections.text: Caution must be taken when splinting to ensure that it is not wrapped too tightly. If wrapped too tightly, the splint may cut off circulation below the splint. If there is numbness, tingling or increased pain, or if the fingers or toes turn pale or bluish, loosen the bandage. Increased swelling may occur; continued monitoring of the splintered fracture is required.

sections.section: TIER 2 SKILLS FOR THE TREATMENT OF FRACTURES
sections.text: When splinting, first responders or CLS should avoid— • Manipulating the fracture site too much, resulting in pain, additional damage to blood vessels, and nerves. • Securing too tightly and cutting off blood flow. • Failing to immobilize the joint above and below the fracture when possible. • Causing further injury. • Making the casualty uncomfortable during transport or evacuation. • Splinting near or over a wound that has not been properly treated.
Care should be taken on cravat placement. First responders or CLS should not apply a cravat on the fracture site, as the pressure from the cravat could cause additional injury to the fracture site.
The ends of the splint should not be placed against the groin, as this could interfere with blood circulation. Extra padding is used for joints or sensitive areas, such as the groin.

Before splinting a suspected fracture, the first responder or CLS should— • Identify the location of the fracture. • Check the pulse below the fracture. • Watch for signs of poor circulation, including coolness, numbness, or lack of a pulse. • Ensure the ends of the rigid objects are not interfering with blood circulation. • If there are any signs of poor circulation, loosen the splint, reposition, and reapply.

The first responder or CLS should follow the below when applying a leg splint: • Apply the splint to the injured extremity with the limb in the position of function or a normal resting position if possible. • Secure the splint in place with appropriate materials. • Ensure the joints above and below the fracture are immobilized in the splint whenever possible. • Recheck the pulse after applying the splint. • Watch for signs of poor circulation, including coolness, numbness, or lack of a pulse. Ensure the ends of the rigid objects are not interfering with blood circulation. If there are any signs of poor circulation, loosen the splint, reposition, and reapply. • Administering the CWMP as needed. • Document all treatment on a DD Form 1380 and attach it to the casualty. 123

Movement or manipulation of a fractured extremity may result in increased pain. The following will help to reduce the casualty's pain: • If possible, have the casualty support their injured arm while preparing the equipment. • Mold the padded splint using the casualty's unaffected limb to avoid unnecessary manipulation. • Use cravats or gauze bandages to immobilize the fracture and secure the limb to the body to minimize unnecessary movement during transport.

The first responder or CLS should follow the following when applying an arm splint: • Place rigid objects so that one is on each side of the injured arm or forearm. • Positioning the rigid objects so that the joint above the fracture and the joint below the fracture will be immobilized. • Apply padding between the arm and the splint. • Secure the splint with cravats, gauze bandages, strips of cloth, or other securing materials. • If possible, place two cravats above and two below the fracture site. • Use square knots to secure bandages tied away from the body on the splint. • Check pulses lower to the affected extremity before and after the application of the splint. • Administering the CWMP as needed. • Document all treatment on a DD Form 1380 and attach it to the casualty.

Splints may be improvised from such items such as boards, poles, sticks, tree limbs, or cardboard. If nothing is available for a splint, the chest wall can be used to immobilize a fractured arm, and the uninjured leg can be used to immobilize (to some extent) the fractured leg.

Padding may be improvised from such items as a jacket, blanket, poncho, shelter half, or leafy vegetation. Padding when splinting a fracture is essential for the well-being of the casualty. It promotes comfort, even pressure distribution, stability, protection against skin issues, and helps manage swelling, all of which contributes to an effective and safer management of fractures, especially in situations where immediate medical care may not be readily available.

Bandages may be improvised from belts, rifle slings, handkerchiefs, or strips torn from clothing, or blankets. Narrow materials such as wire, or cord should not be used to secure a splint in place. The application of wire or narrow material to an extremity could cause tissue damage and a TQ effect.

A sling is a bandage suspended from the neck to support an upper extremity. If a bandage is not available, a sling can be improvised by using the tail of a coat, shirt, or pieces of cloth torn from such items as clothing and blankets. The cravat is ideal for this purpose. Remember that the casualty's hand should be higher than their elbow, and their fingers should be always showing. The sling should be applied so that the supporting pressure is on the uninjured side.

Swathes are any bands (pieces of cloth or straps) that are used to further immobilize a splinted fracture. Cravats are often used and are called swathe bandages. The purpose of the swathe is to immobilize; therefore, the swathe bandage is placed above or below the fracture, not on top of the fracture.

Before beginning first aid procedures for a fracture, gather whatever splinting materials are available. Ensure that splints are long enough to immobilize the joint above and below the suspected fracture. If possible, use at least four ties (two above and two below the fracture) to secure the splints. The ties should be square knots and should be tied away from the body on the splint. Distal pulses of the affected extremity should be checked before and after the application of the splint.

Evaluate the casualty and be prepared to perform any necessary lifesaving measures. Monitor the casualty for development of conditions that may require you to perform necessary lifesaving measures. 124 Fractures and Splinting

Locate the site of the suspected fracture by: • Asking the casualty— ▪ Where are you injured? ▪ Do they have any pain? ▪ Where is it tender? ▪ Can you move the extremity? Note. With the presence of an obvious deformity, do not make the casualty move the extremity. • • Look for an unnatural position of the extremity. Look for a bone sticking out (protruding).

Prepare the casualty for splinting the suspected fracture. • Reassure the casualty. Tell them that you will be providing first aid for them, and that medical help is on the way. • Loosen any tight or binding clothing. • Remove all jewelry from the injured part and place it in the casualty's pocket. Tell the casualty you are doing this because if the jewelry is not removed and swelling occurs later, they may not be able remove it and further bodily injury could result. • Boots should not be removed from the casualty unless they are needed to stabilize a neck injury, or there is actual bleeding from the foot.

Gather splinting materials. If splinting materials (splints, padding, and cravats) are not available, gather improvised materials. If splinting materials are not available and the suspected fracture cannot be splinted, then swathes or a combination of swathes and slings can be used to immobilize the extremity.

Pad the Splints. Pad the splints where they touch any bony part of the body, such as the elbow, wrist, knee, ankle, crotch, or armpit areas. Padding prevents excessive pressure on the area, which could lead to circulation problems.

Check the circulation below the site of the injury. • Note any pale, white, or bluish-gray color of the skin, which may indicate impaired circulation. • Check the temperature of the injured extremity. Use your hand to compare the temperature of the injured side with the uninjured side. The body area below the injury may be colder to the touch indicating poor circulation. • Question the casualty about the presence of numbness, tightness, cold, or tingling sensations. 125

Apply the splint in place by— • Splinting the fracture in the position found. DO NOT attempt to reposition or straighten the injury. If it is an open fracture, stop the bleeding and protect the wound. • Covering all wounds with field dressings before applying a splint. Remember to use the casualty's field dressing, before using your own. • Placing one splint on each side of the fracture. Make sure that the splints reach, if possible, beyond the joints above and below the fracture. • Tying the splints by— ▪ Securing each splint in place above and below the fracture site with cravats, or improvised material. Improvised materials, such as gauze bandage, strips of cloth, belts, or whatever other materials you have, may be used. ▪ With minimal motion to the injured areas, place and tie the splints with the bandages. ▪ Push splint material through and under the natural body curvatures, and then gently position splint material, and tie in place. ▪ Using square knots. Tie all knots on the splint away from the casualty (figure 13-3). DO NOT tie knots directly over the suspected fracture site.

Check the splint for tightness— • CHECK to ensure that the bandages are tight enough to securely hold splinting materials in place, but not so tight that circulation is impaired. • RECHECK the circulation after application of the splint. Check the skin color and temperature. This is to ensure that the bandages holding the splint in place have not been tied too tightly. A fingertip check can be made by inserting the tip of the finger between the bandaged knot and the skin. • MAKE any necessary adjustments without allowing the splint to become ineffective. 126 Fractures and Splinting

An improvised sling may be made from any available non-stretching piece of cloth, such as a utility uniform shirt or trousers, poncho, or shelter half. Slings may also be improvised using the tail of a coat (figure 13-4), belt (figure 13-5), or a piece of cloth may also be used for support. A sling is used to place the supporting pressure on the casualty's uninjured side (figure 13-6). The hand on the supported arm is positioned slightly higher than the elbow, showing the fingers. for support for support

The sling is secured by bringing the ends of the sling up and tie them at the side (or hollow) of the neck on the uninjured side (figure 13-7). The end or corner of the sling is then twisted and tucked at the elbow (figure 13-8). tied to the side of neck twisted and tucked at the elbow

Apply swathes to the injured arm by wrapping the swathe over the injured arm, around the casualty's back, and under the arm on the uninjured side. Tie the ends on the uninjured side (figure 13-9 on page 128). You may use any large piece of cloth, Service member's belt, or pistol belt, to improvise a swathe. A swathe is applied to an injured leg by wrapping the swathe around both legs and securing it on the uninjured side. 127
Seek medical assistance. Notify medical personnel, watch closely for development of life-threatening conditions and, or impaired circulation to the injured extremity.

Splinting or immobilizing a fracture is essential for providing immediate and effective care to casualties in a tactical environment. It contributes to stabilizing the injury, managing pain, preventing complications, and facilitating safe evacuation, ultimately improving the chances of a positive outcome for the injured individual.
To splint an upper extremity fracture— • Have the casualty sit up. • Have someone support the fractured extremity. • Remove all jewelry from the fractured extremity. • Expose the fracture site.

Figure 13-10 on page 129 through figure 13-18 on page 131 shows you how to apply slings, splints, and cravats (swathes) to immobilize and support fractures of the upper extremities. Although the padding is not visible in some of the illustrations, it is always preferable to apply padding along the injured part for the length of the splint, especially where it touches any bony parts of the body. 128 Fractures and Splinting by twisting and tucking the corner of the sling at the elbow fractured elbow when the elbow is not bent (two methods) 129 arm fracture when no splint is available sling, and cravat used to immobilize the fractured elbow when the elbow is bent shirt and strips of material 130 Fractures and Splinting Immobilizing a Lower Extremity Fracture 367B
