To splint a lower extremity fracture— • Have the casualty sit or lie down. • Have another person manually immobilize the fractured extremity. • Remove the footgear and expose the fracture site. • Check distal (at the wrist) pulse and capillary refill on the injured extremity. Prepare the splint for application. Note. Measuring and forming of splints should be done on the unbroken extremity prior to placing on the broken one.

Figure 13-19 on page 132 through figure 13-25 on page 135 show how to apply splints to immobilize fractures of the lower extremities. Although padding is not visible in some of the illustrations, it is always preferable to apply padding along the injured part for the length of the splint, especially where it touches any bony parts of the body. 131 132 Fractures and Splinting 133 lower extremity 134 Fractures and Splinting Immobilizing a Jaw, Collarbone, or Shoulder Fracture 368B

To immobilize a fractured jaw, apply a cravat or gauze bandage following the guidelines outlined in paragraph 11-39 on page 114. Ensure that all bandaging support is directed to the top of the casualty's head rather than the back of their neck. Placing the bandage incorrectly may result in pulling the casualty's jaw backward, potentially obstructing their breathing and exacerbating the injury.
A fractured collarbone can be immobilized by applying two belts, a sling, and a swathe. Figure 13-26 illustrates how to immobilize a fractured collarbone.

A suspected dislocated or fractured shoulder can be immobilized by applying a sling and a swathe. Figure 13-27 on page 136 illustrated how to properly immobilize a dislocated or fractured shoulder. 135 shoulder Immobilizing a Spinal Column Fracture 369B

It is often impossible to be sure if a casualty has a fractured spinal column. Be suspicious of any back injury, especially if the casualty has fallen or if their back has been sharply struck or bent. If a casualty has received such an injury and does not have feeling in their legs or cannot move them, you can be reasonably sure that they have a severe back injury which is managed as a fracture. A neck fracture or injury to the back should always be suspected, and it is often impossible to be sure if a casualty has a fractured spinal column. If the spine is fractured (figure 13-28 step A on page 137), bending it can cause the sharp bone fragments to bruise or cut the spinal cord and result in permanent paralysis or death. The spinal column must maintain normal spinal position at the lower back (lumbar region) to help remove pressure from the spinal cord.

If the casualty is not to be transported until medical personnel arrive— • Caution them not to move. Ask if they are in pain or, if they are unable to move any part of their body. • Leave them in the position in which they were found. DO NOT move any part of their body unless they are in imminent danger. • If the casualty is lying face up, slip a blanket or other supporting material under the arch of their lower back to help support the spine in a normal position (figure 13-28 step B on page 137). Take care not to place so much bulky padding under your casualty, as this will cause potential damage and cause undue pressure on the spine. • If the casualty is lying face down, DO NOT put anything under any part of their body. 136 Fractures and Splinting

If the casualty must be transported to a safe location before medical personnel arrive and if the casualty is in a— • Face-up position, transport them by litter or use a firm substitute, such as a wide board or a door longer than their height. Loosely tie the casualty's wrists together over their waistline, using a cravat, gauze bandage, or a strip of cloth. Tie their feet together to prevent the accidental dropping or shifting of their legs. Lay a folded blanket across the litter where the arch of their back is to be placed. Using a four-person team (figure 13-29 on page 138), place the casualty on the litter without bending their spinal column or their neck. Avoid prolonged use, temporary if possible. 137 • • • • • The number two Service member positions themself at the casualty's head. Their responsibility is to provide manual in-line (neutral) stabilization of the head and neck. The number three, and four Service members position themselves on one side of the casualty; all kneel on one knee along the uninjured side of the casualty. The number one Service member positions themself preferably to the opposite side of the casualty as the number three and four members. The number one member can be on the same side as number three and four, if needed. Numbers two, three, and four Service members gently place their hands under the casualty. The number one Service member on the opposite side places their hands under the injured part to assist. When all four Service members are in position to lift, the number two Service member commands, "PREPARE TO LIFT" and then, "LIFT." On th

Casualties in a facedown position must be transported in the facedown position. The four-person team lifts the casualty onto a regular or improvised litter, keeping the spinal column in a normal spinal position. If a regular litter is used, first place a folded blanket on the litter at the point where the chest will be placed. 138 Fractures and Splinting Immobilizing a Neck Fracture 370B

A fractured neck is extremely dangerous. Bone fragments may bruise or cut the spinal cord just as they might in a fractured back. If the casualty is not to be transported until medical personnel arrive— • Caution them not to move. Moving may cause permanent injury or death. • Leave the casualty in the position in which they are found. If their neck and head (cervical spine) are in an abnormal position, immediately immobilize the neck and head. • Keep their head still, if the casualty is lying face up, raise their shoulders slightly, and slip a roll of cloth that has the bulk of a bath towel under their neck (figure 13-30). The roll should be thick enough to arch their neck only slightly, leaving the back of their head on the ground. DO NOT bend their neck or head forward. DO NOT raise or twist their head. • Immobilize the casualty's head (figure 13-31). Do this by padding heavy objects (such as rocks or their boots filled with dirt, sand, gravel, or rock) and placing them on each side of their head. If it is necessary to use boots, after filling them, tie the top tightly or stuff with pieces of cloth to secure the contents. (bulk) under neck neck with boots
DO NOT move the casualty if they are lying face down. Immobilize the head and neck by padding heavy objects and placing them on each side of their head. DO NOT put a roll of cloth under the neck.

DO NOT bend the neck or head, nor roll the casualty onto their back. If the casualty must be prepared for transportation before medical personnel arrive at least two persons are needed to move the casualty's head and trunk in unison.

Care is taken should a casualty have to be moved prior to medical personnel arrival. The casualty is prepared by— • A wide board is placed lengthwise beside the casualty. It should extend at least 4 inches beyond the casualty's head and feet (figure 13-32 step A on page 140). Avoid prolonged use, if possible. • If the casualty is lying face up, the number one Service member steadies the casualty's head and neck between their hands. At the same time, the number two Service member positions one foot and one knee against the board to prevent it from slipping. They then grasp the casualty underneath their shoulder and hip and gently slide the casualty onto the board (figure 13-32 step B on page 140). • If the casualty is lying face down, the number one member steadies the casualty's head and neck between their hands, while the number two Service member gently rolls the casualty over onto the board (figure 13-32 step C on page 140). • The number one Service member continues to steady the casualty's head and neck. The number two Service member simultaneously raises the casualty's shoulders slightly, places padding under their neck, and immobilizes the casualty's head. Any improvised supports are secured in position with a cravat, gauze bandage, or strip of cloth extended across the casualty's forehead and under the board (figure 13-32 step D on page 140). • The board is lifted onto a litter or blanket in order to transport the casualty (figure 13-32 step E). 139 140

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: Because medical personnel will not always be readily available, nonmedical personnel must rely on themselves and other Service members' knowledge and fundamentals of first aid for secondary injuries until medical assistance is gained and initiated. This section will provide additional first aid, non-TCCC, procedures that nonmedical personnel can use in a garrison environment, or in combat situations.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: The most serious abdominal wound is one in which an object penetrates the abdominal wall and pierces internal organs or large blood vessels. In these instances, bleeding may be severe, and death can occur rapidly.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: The first step in treating an abdominal wound is to position the casualty. Place and maintain the casualty on their back with their knees in an upright (flexed) position (figure 14-1). The knees-up position helps relieve pain, assists in the treatment of shock, prevents further exposure of the bowel (intestines) or abdominal organs, and helps relieve abdominal pressure by allowing the abdominal muscles to relax.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: Expose the wound by— • Removing the casualty's loose clothing to expose the wound. However, DO NOT attempt to remove clothing that is stuck to the wound; removing it may cause further injury. • Gently pick up any organs that may be on the ground. Do this with a clean, dry dressing or with the cleanest available material. Place the organs on top of the casualty's abdomen (figure 14-2). 141 Note. DO NOT probe, clean, or try to remove any foreign object from the abdomen. DO NOT touch with bare hands any exposed organs. DO NOT push organs back inside the body.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: It may be necessary to wear improvised dressing (for example strips of cloth, a t-shirt, or the cleanest material available). Stabilize any protruding or impaled objects and apply a sterile abdominal dressing as follows: Note. Protruding abdominal organs should be kept moist to prevent the tissue from drying out. A moist sterile dressing should be applied if available. • • • • • • Using the sterile side of the dressing, or other clean material, place any protruding organs near the wound. (DO NOT try to push organs back inside the body.) Ensure that the dressing is large enough to cover the entire mass of protruding organs or area of the wound. If large enough to cover the affected area, place the sterile side of the plastic wrapper directly over the wound. Moisten the dressing with clean water prior to placing a dressing over the exposed organs. Place the dressing directly on top of the wound or plastic wrapper, if used. Tie the dressings loosely at the casualty's side.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: If two dressings are needed to cover a large wound, repeat steps in paragraph 15-5. If necessary, loosely cover the dressing with a cravat, elastic bandage, or gauze bandage. Tie them on the side of the casualty opposite to that of the dressing ties.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: To avoid causing further injury to the casualty— • Do not touch any exposed organs. • Do not try to push any exposed organs back into the body. • Do not tie the dressing tails tightly or directly over the wound. • Do not give the casualty anything by mouth. Note. Continue to evaluate the casualty and provide necessary first aid.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: Prepare the casualty for evacuation as follows: • Place the casualty on their back (face up) with the knees flexed. • Keep the patient warm, cover with a blanket as needed. • If evacuation is delayed, check the casualty for shock every five minutes. • Seek medical aid. • Record the procedures applied on DD Form 1380.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: The first responder continues to evaluate the casualties and is prepared to perform basic first aid measures. Always check for both entry and exit wounds. If there are two wounds (entry and exit), treat the wound that appears more serious first (for example, the heavier bleeding, protruding organs, larger wound, and so forth). It may be necessary to improvise dressings for the second wound by using strips of cloth, a tshirt, or the cleanest material available.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: Use the casualty's dressing from the first aid kit, not your own. If the dressing is not large enough to cover the entire wound, the plastic wrapper from the dressing may be used to cover the wound first (placing the dressing on top). Open the plastic wrapper carefully without touching the inner surface. If necessary, other improvised dressings may be made from clothing, blankets, or the cleanest materials available.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: Hypothermia prevention measures are taken with abdominal injuries due to the risk of rapid heat loss from the exposed abdominal cavity or organs. Moisten the dressing with clean water prior to placing a dressing over the exposed organs and seeking medical assistance. 142 Expedient Techniques for other Secondary Injuries

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: Expedient bandaging techniques are of paramount importance for the U.S. military due to their ability to provide immediate and effective medical care in combat situations. In the fast-paced and unpredictable nature of military operations, Service members often face severe injuries that require immediate attention to stabilize the wounded and prevent further harm. Expedient bandaging techniques enable military personnel to apply life-saving measures to control bleeding and increase the chances of survival for injured personnel. These techniques not only buy valuable time until medical help arrives but also contribute to the overall mission readiness by ensuring that Service members can continue their duties with confidence and knowing that essential medical support is readily available when needed.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: To apply shoulder bandages attached to the field first aid dressing— • Take one bandage across the chest, the other across the back, and under the arm opposite the injured shoulder. • Tie the ends with a square knot (figure 14-3 on page 144). • Ensure that the bandages are snug but not too tight, allowing for proper circulation and comfort for the casualty. 143

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: To apply a bandage to the shoulder or armpit— • Make an extended bandage by using two cravats or an elastic bandage (figure 14-4 step A on page 145); place the end of the first cravat along the base of the second one (figure 14-4 step B on page 145). • Fold the two bandages into a single extended bandage (figure 14-4 step C on page 145). • Fold the extended bandage into a single cravat (figure 14-4 step D on page 145). After folding, secure the thicker part (overlap) with tape or two or more safety pins (figure 14-4 step E on page 145). • Place the middle of the cravat under the armpit so that the front end is longer than the back end and safety pins are on the outside (figure 14-4 step F on page 145). • Cross the ends on top of the shoulder (figure 14-4 step G on page 145). • Take one of the bandages, which ends across the back and under the arm on the opposite side and the other end across the chest. Tie the ends (figure 14-4 step H on page 145).

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: Be sure to place sufficient wadding in the armpit. DO NOT tie the bandage too tightly. Avoid compressing the major blood vessels in the armpit. 144 Expedient Techniques for other Secondary Injuries

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: To apply a cravat to the elbow— • Bend the arm at the elbow and place the middle of the cravat at the point of the elbow bringing the ends upward (figure 14-5 step A on page 146). • Bring the ends across, extending both downward (figure 14-5 step B on page 146). • Take both ends around the arm and tie them with a square knot at the front of the elbow (figure 14-5 step C on page 146). 145

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: To apply a bandage to the hand— • Place the hand in the middle of the cravat or gauze bandage with the wrist at the base of the bandage (figure 14-6 step A). Ensure that the fingers are separated with absorbent material to prevent chafing and irritation of the skin. • Place the apex over the fingers and tuck any excess material into the pleats on each side of the hand (figure 14-6 step B). • Cross the ends on top of the hand, take them around the wrist, and tie them (figure 14-6 step C through step E) with a square knot. 146 Expedient Techniques for other Secondary Injuries

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: To apply a bandage to the palm of the hand— • Lay the middle of the cravat or gauze bandage over the palm of the hand with the ends hanging down on each side (figure 14-7 step A). • Take the end of the cravat or gauze bandage at the little finger across the back of the hand, extending this upward over the base of the thumb; then bring it downward across the palm (figure 14-7 step B). • Take the thumb end across the back of the hand, over the palm, and through the hollow between the thumb and palm (figure 14-7 step C). • Take the ends to the back of the hand and cross them; then bring them up over the wrist and cross them again (figure 14-7 step D). • Bring both ends down and tie them with a square knot on top of the wrist (figure 14-7 step E through step F).

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: To apply a bandage to the leg— • Place the center of the cravat or gauze bandage over the dressing (figure 14-8 step A on page 148). • Take one end around and up the leg in a spiral motion and the other end around and down the leg in a spiral motion, overlapping part of each preceding turn (figure 14-8 step B on page 148). • Bring both ends together and tie them (figure 14-8 step C on page 148) with a square knot. 147

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: To apply a bandage to the knee as illustrated in figure 14-9, use the same technique applied in bandaging the elbow described in paragraph 14-16 on page 145.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: To apply a bandage to the foot— 148 Expedient Techniques for other Secondary Injuries • • • Place the foot in the middle of the cravat, elastic bandage, or gauze bandage with the heel well forward of the base (figure 14-10 step A). Ensure that the toes are separated by absorbent material to prevent chafing and irritation of the skin. Place the apex over the top of the foot and tuck any excess material into the pleats on each side of the foot (figure 14-10 step B). Cross the ends on top of the foot, take them around the ankle, and tie them at the front of the ankle (figure 14-10 step C through step E).

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: Depending upon where the impaled object is located on the body, extreme care must be exercised. Improper methods may cause severe injury and possess the potential for further disability and death.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: Apply first aid for an impaled object as follows: • Tell the casualty to remain still and not to move the impaled object. • Expose the injury by cutting away or removing the clothing or equipment around the wound site. • If the impalement is on an extremity, check the pulse distal (situated away from the center of the body or injury) from the injury site. Note. If an assistant is available, one person should immobilize the object while the other applies the dressings and bandages. • • • • • • • If necessary, apply direct pressure using gloved hands on either side of the object. Place several layers of bulky dressings around the injury site so that the dressings surround the object. Use additional bulky materials or dressings to build up the area around the object. Apply the support bandages. Apply the bandage over the bulky support material to hold it in place. Apply the bandage tightly but not so tightly as to impair circulation or breathing. Check circulation after applying the support bandages. Note. If a pulse was felt on an extremity and cannot be felt after the bandage has been applied, the bandage must be loosened until a pulse can be felt. 149 • • • • Immobilize the affected area with a splint or sling, if applicable. Check for a pulse distal (far side of the wound) to the injury site. Treat for shock, if necessary. Seek medical assistance.

sections.chapter: Expedient techniques for other secondary injuries
sections.text: If the impalement is found in the cheek and both ends of the object can be seen, perform the following: • Remove the object in the direction it entered the cheek. • Position the casualty to allow for drainage. • If both ends of the object in the cheek cannot be seen, immobilize the impaled object. 150

After the first responder and CLS have treated the casualty in CUF and TFC phase of TCCC they may be required to continue to monitor the casualty and prepare the casualty for evacuation. The first responder and CLS cannot treat a casualty and then forget about them. The casualty must be continually monitored and reassessed prior to the casualty's evacuation. The continued monitoring utilizing the MARCH-PAWS sequence will allow the first responder and CLS to identify changes in the casualty's condition and initiate those interventions necessary to prevent unnecessary death.

Casualty monitoring follows the same MARCH-PAWS process and will guide the first responder and CLS through their reassessments. After the initial casualty assessment and any treatments that are performed, the casualty must be reassessed every 15 minutes, or if seriously wounded every five to 10 minutes. The reassessment should start by reexamining any massive bleeding issues or interventions, should proceed through the rest of the MARCH-PAWS sequence, and be repeated until that casualty is transferred to the care of medical personnel.

The first responder or CLS should next evaluate any changes in respiratory status, look for signs or symptoms of shock, hypothermia, or head injuries. Also, monitor the casualty's respiratory rate, pulse, and level of consciousness. Assessing the casualty's respiratory status involves checking the rate and the quality of the respirations. By looking, listening, and feeling for breaths on the cheek, the respiratory rate can be determined (documented in the number of breaths per minute) and the respiratory effort (shallow breaths, difficulties moving air in and out, and loss of air movement on one side of the chest).

If a casualty becomes unconscious or breathing rate drops below eight respirations within one minute, insert an NPA. The casualty must be reassessed for tension pneumothorax and treated as necessary by performing an NDC. The NDC must be reassessed to confirm that it was successful. Document the rate, respiratory effort, and time assessed on DD Form 1380. If the casualty's respiratory status begins to change, reassess their status using the same approach used in the tactical trauma assessment.

The level of consciousness is best expressed by addressing the casualty's response using the AVPU method. Document any AVPU assessments or any changes in the casualty's status on the DD Form 1380. This documentation helps medical personnel better understand the casualty's situation. Note. If the casualty is not ALERT, indicating decreased mental status, the casualty should not have weapons or communications equipment.

Assessing the casualty's circulation status is done by checking for pulses. Depending on the casualty and their injuries, the first responder and CLS can check the casualty's pulse at the carotid artery (neck) or radial artery (wrist). The first responder and CLS should use their index and middle fingers, NOT their thumb, to check pulses (figure 15-1 on page 152). Document pulse rates, locations, and time taken on the DD Form 1380. Note. The absence of a radial pulse is an indication that the casualty is in shock. 151

When requesting MEDEVAC, several preparatory actions are crucial for ensuring the casualty's safety and stability during transport. These steps include: • Securing the Casualty's Weapons and Equipment: It is vital to secure all weapons and equipment according to the SOPs or mission requirements. Due to the potential inability of casualties to manage their own equipment owing to injuries or altered mental status, it is essential to secure these items to prevent accidents. If possible, weapons should not accompany the casualty during evacuation. If securing the weapon is not feasible, ensure it is cleared and rendered safe. • Selecting Appropriate Litter: Choose a litter that aligns with both the casualty's specific needs and the mission profile to facilitate a safe and efficient evacuation. • Preparing Equipment for Evacuation: Organize and prepare any equipment that is needed to accompany the casualty. This includes medical supplies or specialized gear necessary for their condition. • Anticipating Environmental Factors: Consider environmental challenges that might impact the casualty's stability during evacuation. This includes extreme noises, vibrations from the transport vehicle, high winds from propeller wash, and exposure to cold temperatures due to altitude or the environment. • Developing a Mitigation Plan: Formulate a plan to address each potential environmental threat to maintain the casualty's stability throughout the evacuation process.

It is important to note that medical personnel receiving the casualty may not be familiar with the equipment or have the means to secure it. Thus, preparing adequately and ensuring everything is in order prior to evacuation is critical for the safety and care of the casualty.

Pre-evacuation procedures bridge both TFC and Tactical Evacuation Care. Immediate life-threatening hemorrhage control, followed by the prevention and treatment of other injuries and complications have all been completed before most pre-evacuation procedures are initiated. Although, some of the communication and documentation may be ongoing during the TFC phase.

When providing care, the first responder or CLS should always talk to the injured person. Getting hurt can cause a lot of worry and fear, on top of the stress from combat. It helps to speak openly with them about what injuries they have and what you're doing to help. Let them know that you're doing everything possible for them and assure them that they're in good hands. This kind of support can help lessen their anxiety.

It's important to be truthful about the injuries but keep a hopeful tone when talking about rescue and treatment. Chatting with the injured person is not only comforting but also lets you check how they are feeling mentally. Explaining what you're doing as you provide care can boost both your own confidence and the injured person's trust in you. 152 Casualty Monitoring and Evacuation Preparation

Communicate with leaders as soon as possible and throughout casualty treatment. Leaders need to understand the impact of casualties on the mission. Communicate with medical providers about details of the casualty injuries. This includes 9-line communication and ongoing MIST reports. Communication is also important, as the injured casualty may affect the success of the mission or change the tactical landscape.

Medical documentation may be difficult to accomplish in tactical prehospital settings, but it is important to the casualty's subsequent care that every effort should be made to document the care provided by first responders and medics throughout the trauma care continuum from point of wounding and injury to definitive care at the hospital. A DD Form 1380 is provided in each first aid kit.

Based on the principles of TCCC, this card provides an easy way to document initial lifesaving care provided at the point of wounding. The card also serves as a prompt to remind first responders and CLS of the assessment and treatment steps of the MARCH-PAWS sequence. DD Form 1380 is relatively selfexplanatory once personnel have been trained on using the form.

The MIST information about the casualty informs the MEDEVAC request and can be collected simultaneously with the other required information. The MIST report transmits medical information to the receiving combat medic, evacuation platform, and MTF to better prepare for specific inbound casualties. A MIST report conveys additional evacuation information that may be required by commanders.

Transitioning casualty care to another medical team is best accomplished with an oral discussion of the casualty's status, along with the written documentation on the DD Form 1380. When an oral hand-off is not a viable option, the written information may be the only way receiving medical personnel will know what the provider has done to help the casualty and what the next steps should be to provide the best care going forward.

The DD Form 1380 (figure 15-2 on page 154) should be completed on every casualty before handoff to another provider or evacuation to an MTF. DD Form 1380 will follow the patient and will be used until the patient arrives at a role of care where a DD Form 3019 (Resuscitation Record), can be used. Note 1. This document should remain with the casualty throughout the prehospital evacuation system and become part of the casualty's medical record upon reaching an MTF. The data from the DD Form 1380 will also be uploaded into the DOD Trauma Registry maintained by the JTS. Note 2. Many commercially available casualty cards do not replicate all information requirements of the DD Form 1380. While the DD Form 1380 may be reproduced locally, it should be on waterproof paper or laminated with a means of attaching it to the casualty. It is best to have an indelible or permanent marker available for writing on the TCCC Card. 153 Legend:

All Service members should have at least one or more DD Form 1380s within their first aid kit. For additional information and instructions on completing the DD Form 1380 refer to AR 40-66. Use the following steps to complete a DD Form 1380: • Remove the DD Form 1380 from the casualty's first aid kit. • Complete all entries as fully as possible. Note. As the DD Form 1380 is the first, and sometimes the only record of treatment of combat casualties, accuracy and thoroughness of information provided is of the utmost importance. • 154 Front of DD Form 1380 (figure 15-2): ▪ Battle Roster # - Write first letter of the casualty's first name, then write first letter of the casualty's last name, write the last four numbers of the casualty's identification number. In figure 15-2, the Service member's battle roster number is "BL6553." Casualty Monitoring and Evacuation Preparation ▪ • Evacuation (EVAC) - Mark an "X" on the casualty's evacuation precedence (Urgent; Priority; or Routine). ▪ Name - Write casualty's name (Last, First). ▪ Last 4 - Write last four numbers of casualty's identification number. ▪ Sex - Mark an "X" on the casualty's sex Male (M) or Female (F). ▪ Date - Write date of injury in DD-MMM-YY format. For example, "29-JUN-13." ▪ Time - Write 24-hour time of injury and indicate whether Local (L) or Zulu (Z) time. For example, "1300Z." ▪ Service - Write casualty's branch of service (United States Army [USA], United States Air Force [USAF], United States Coast Guard [USCG], United States Navy [USN], United States Marine Corps [USMC], and United States Space Force [USSF].

First responders and CLS personnel are advised to fill out the DD Form 1380 to the best of their ability. DD Form 1380 is crucial as it records evidence of initial treatment and provides subsequent levels of medical care with essential information. This documentation is vital for medical personnel to assess and determine the appropriate continuation of care for the casualty. This process ensures that each step of medical intervention is informed and based on prior actions taken, facilitating a cohesive and effective treatment pathway.

Every Service member should be able to initiate a 9-line MEDEVAC request. The standard MEDEVAC request has nine lines. However, lines one through five are required before a MEDEVAC can be launched. Using a phonetic alphabet and following the unit's normal communications procedures, call in: • Grid location. • Radio frequency and call sign. • Number of casualties by precedence. • Equipment that needs to be brought by the evacuation team. • Number of litter and ambulatory casualties.
Before initiating a 9-line MEDEVAC request, collect all the information needed. When calling in, be sure to follow all appropriate communication protocols and guidance.

Depending on operational, mission variables, and availability, evacuation options may involve MEDEVAC, CASEVAC, or a combination of the two. During CASEVAC, casualties are moved without medical regulating and do not possess a protected status under the Geneva Conventions. As such, CASEVAC platforms may be engaged by enemy forces. With MEDEVAC, patients may be regulated or unregulated and the ambulance is properly marked, MEDEVAC cannot be used for nonmedical missions without losing its protected status. The 9-line MEDEVAC request is communicated through the designated evacuation system or Patient Evacuation Coordination Cell, depending on orders and the tactical SOP.

When a Service member requests a MEDEVAC, they are not directly coordinating with a medical provider but are explaining the requestor's evacuation requirements with someone who coordinates the movement assets. Although they still require some general information about the status of the casualty, much of the information that they need to coordinate evacuation is not clinical and relates to logistical and operational issues.

Communicate with medical providers on the evacuation asset if possible and relay the MIST report. Provide additional information as appropriate. For additional information on MEDEVAC request refer to ATP 4-02.2. 156 Casualty Monitoring and Evacuation Preparation

Essential evacuation equipment (for example, litters, packaging materials, and BVMs) should be prepared by other unit personnel while medical treatment continues and coordinating with the casualty treatment team to save time. For example, other unit members can prepare litters while treatment is being provided. Do not delay getting casualties onto litters. The first responder and CLS can better prevent hypothermia by getting casualties off the ground.

Casualty movement in TFC may be better accomplished using litter due to the tactical situation and the need to move casualties rapidly. The litter exists only to facilitate casualty movement, and the casualty can be placed in the best position that facilitates their care and comfort. Casualties do not have to be placed on their backs on a litter. It is easier to move them if they are already on the litter; however, they must be secured to the litter before movement. Litter is also usually better for moving a casualty long distance.

All unit members should know how to open and set up litters and rehearse their use during pre-mission training. All unit members should know who will carry litter or where litter is located on vehicles.

Selecting the proper litter is dependent on several different factors: • The evacuation platform. • The terrain at the location of pick-up. • The casualty's injuries. • The availability of different types of litters.

Two of the more common litters often used are the quad-folding litter and the lightweight flexible stretchers. Each of them has advantages and disadvantages and maybe the proper litter depends on the situation. For example, flexible litter can be moved using a one-person drag (terrain permitting) but are more difficult to carry longer distances than a quad-folding litter.

Each unit will have litters that have been proven to support their mission profile, and it is important to be aware of the limitations and advantages of each litter at your disposal before being deployed in a situation where you will require them.

When preparing a casualty for evacuation, the first responder or CLS need to anticipate the environmental factors that could prevent the casualty from remaining stable. Examples include extreme noises, vibrations, high winds from propeller washing, and exposure to cold environments from either altitude or low ambient temperatures. A plan should be developed to mitigate each of those potential threats when preparing for your casualty.

All loose ends of bandages, medical equipment, and hypothermia prevention materials should be secured. The first responder or CLS should prevent dressings and other medical items from being blown around by the rotor wash or becoming entangled with other equipment.

Loose materials can catch on anything from tree limbs to body-armor of litter bearers, to parts of the aircraft or vehicles. Any snag like this can cause delays in evacuation or even further injury to casualties or providers. Blankets and foil-based hypothermia materials are especially susceptible to being caught in the wind.

Hypothermia prevention equipment should be tucked and secured beneath the casualty and litter straps. Loose edges can be caught up in wind or rotor wash or snagged on objects in the helicopter as the casualty is loaded aboard.
The TQs should remain visible and not be hidden. The DD Form 1380 should be attached to the casualty. 157 Evacuation Considerations for Suspected Spinal Injuries 371B

A spinal injury should be expected in certain situations, like fast-roping falls or being near a significant blast. In those cases, when tactically feasible, ensure the C-spine is immobilized and the casualty is kept straight during evacuation. Keep the litter type and evacuation platform in mind and ensure the evacuation ground or air vehicle can accommodate the selected litter.

Not all casualties require a litter for evacuation. For those casualties who are still ambulatory, provide instructions or assistance as needed. Depending on the nature of their injuries, they may be able to assist with carrying litters or providing security.

It is best to guide disoriented or visually impaired casualties by having them place their hand on the shoulder of the casualty in front of them, or a nonmedical attendant as they move to the evacuation platform. Instruct them on repeatedly checking their own wounds and dressings to ensure that bleeding remains controlled throughout the evacuation process.

A particular importance when moving more than one casualty is the process of staging the casualties. Based on the guidance from the MEDEVAC personnel, certain casualties have priority and may need to be loaded last, so that they are the first ones offloaded at the destination.

If not given specific guidance, place the most serious casualty in a position where they are loaded last, and have casualties who may be less severely injured loaded before them. The first responder or CLS may also need to assist in marking the LZ, providing security, or assisting in marshalling the aircraft or litterbearer teams.

It is critical that documentation of personnel, injury, and treatment be annotated using DD Form 1380 and should be completed prior to any handoff of the casualty. If care cannot be documented using the DD Form 1380 at the point of care by the first responder or CLS, it should be documented using the TCCC after action review, found on the JTS website, as soon as possible (within 72 hours) after treatment. The nonmedical first responder or CLS should follow up with the supporting unit medical personnel to complete and submit the TCCC after action review. 158

Bites and stings are common occurrences that can happen in almost every environment. From pesky mosquito bites to venomous snakebites, these encounters with creatures big and small can lead to a range of discomfort, pain, and even potential danger. Understanding the various types of bites and stings, their causes, and proper treatment is crucial for minimizing the associated risks and ensuring a swift recovery.

Poison and venom are terms often used interchangeably, but they have distinct differences in their mode of delivery and the way they affect living organisms. A poison is a substance that is harmful or lethal when ingested, inhaled, or absorbed through the skin. It is typically produced by plants, animals, or microorganisms as a defensive mechanism. Poisonous substances can be found in various forms, such as toxins in certain plants, chemicals in household products, or even certain medications when taken in excessive amounts. The key characteristic of poison is that it needs to be ingested or absorbed into the body to cause harm.

Venom is a specialized secretion that is actively injected into another organism. It is typically produced by certain animals, such as snakes, spiders, scorpions, and some insects. Venom is delivered through specialized organs, such as fangs, stingers, or spines, and is primarily used for hunting or self-defense. Unlike poison, venom is actively injected into the victim's bloodstream, tissues, or body cavities, often leading to localized or systemic effects, which can range from pain and swelling to paralysis or even death. The main distinction between poison and venom lies in their delivery method. Poison is harmful when ingested or absorbed, while venom is specifically injected into another organism through specialized organs.

If bites and stings are not treated promptly and correctly, they may cause serious illness or death. The severity of a snakebite depends upon whether the snake is venomous or nonvenomous, the type of snake, the location of the bite, and the amount of venom injected. Bites from humans and other animals, such as dogs, cats, bats, raccoons, and rats, can cause severe bruises and infection and tears or lacerations of tissue. Awareness of the potential sources of injuries can reduce or prevent them from occurring. Knowledge and prompt application of first aid measures can lessen the severity of injuries from bites and stings and keep the Service member from becoming a serious casualty. 159

First aid for human or animal bites aims to prevent infection and provide initial care for the wound. To perform first aid for a human or animal bite: • Remove yourself from further harm. If dealing with an animal bite, ensure that you are no longer at risk of being bitten again. • Control bleeding. If the bite wound is bleeding, apply direct pressure with a clean cloth or sterile gauze to stop or minimize the bleeding. Elevating the wound, if possible, can also help reduce bleeding. • Clean the wound. Rinse the bite wound thoroughly with clean water or saline solution to flush out any dirt, bacteria, or saliva that may have entered the wound. Gently remove any debris from the wound using mild soap and water. • Apply an antiseptic. After cleaning, apply an antiseptic solution or ointment to the wound to help reduce the risk of infection. Follow the instructions on the product label and ensure it is suitable for use on open wounds. • Cover the wound. Use a sterile dressing or clean bandage to cover the wound. This will protect it from further contamination and promote healing. Change dressing regularly to maintain cleanliness. • Seek medical attention. It is important to seek medical evaluation for all animal bites, especially those from unfamiliar or wild animals, deep wounds, or those that become red, swollen, or increasingly painful. A health care professional can assess the severity of the bite, prescribe antibiotics if necessary, and administer tetanus prophylaxis if required.

If someone gets bitten by an animal, whether known, unknown, wild, or domestic, the primary concern is rabies. Unless the animal is someone's pet and verified to be up to date on rabies, the individual who has been bitten must get the rabies post-exposure vaccine. Seemingly minor bites can lead to infection, so it is essential to consult a health care professional to determine the appropriate course of action and receive any necessary medical treatment. Note. If unable to capture or kill the animal, provide medical personnel with any information that will help identify it.

Except for sharks and barracuda, most marine animals will not deliberately attack. The most frequent injuries from marine animals are wounds by biting, stinging, or puncturing. Wounds inflicted by marine animals can be very painful but are rarely fatal.

Wounds from sharks, barracuda, and crocodilian can involve major trauma because of bites and lacerations. Bites from large marine animals are potentially the most life-threatening of all injuries from marine animals. Major wounds from these animals can be treated by controlling the bleeding, preventing shock, giving basic life support, splinting the injury, and by securing prompt medical aid.
Turtles, moray eels, and corals normally inflict minor wounds. Treat by cleansing the wound(s) thoroughly and by splinting if necessary.

Jellyfish, anemones, and others marine animals inflict injury by means of stinging cells in their tentacles. Contact with the tentacles produces burning pain with a rash and small hemorrhages on the skin. Shock, muscular cramping, nausea, vomiting, and respiratory distress may also occur. Gently remove the clinging tentacles with a towel and wash or treat the area. Use diluted ammonia or alcohol, a meat tenderizer, and talcum powder. If symptoms become severe or persist, seek medical assistance.

Spiny fish, urchins, stingrays, and cone shells inject their venom by puncturing the skin with their spines. General signs and symptoms include swelling, nausea, vomiting, generalized cramps, diarrhea, muscular paralysis, and shock. Deaths are rare. Treatment consists of soaking the wound(s) in hot water (when available) for 30 to 60 minutes. This inactivates the heat sensitive toxin. In addition, further first aid measures should be taken such as controlling bleeding or applying a dressing. This should be carried out as necessary. 160 Bites and Stings

Snakebites can occur unexpectedly during outdoor activities or encounters with snakes in their natural habitats. Understanding how to identify snakes, knowing the proper steps to take after a snakebite, and having a grasp of basic first aid techniques can significantly increase the chances of a positive outcome in such situations. Snakes are categorized between nonvenomous and venomous snakes.

Snakes can be categorized into various groups based on different characteristics. One common classification system categorizes snakes into four main categories of colubrid snakes, constrictor snakes, nonvenomous snakes, and venomous snakes. These categories may overlap, and some snakes may possess traits from multiple categories. Understanding the different categories of snakes can aid in snake identification, assessing potential risks, and knowing how to respond appropriately in various situations.

Colubrid snakes represent the largest snake family and include a wide range of non-venomous species. These snakes have diverse habitats, sizes, and feeding habits. Common colubrid snakes include rat, king, gopher, and water snakes.

Constrictor snakes are non-venomous snakes that subdue their prey by coiling around them and squeezing until they can no longer breathe. Constrictors then swallow their prey whole. Well-known constrictor snakes include boas, pythons, and anacondas.

Non-venomous snakes include snakes that lack venom glands or fangs and pose no direct threat to humans. Non-venomous snakes play an essential role in controlling rodent populations and maintaining ecological balance. Examples of non-venomous snakes are boas, pythons, corn, and garter snakes.

There are approximately 130 different varieties of nonvenomous snakes in the U.S. They have ovalshaped heads and round eyes. Unlike venomous snakes, discussed below, nonvenomous snakes do not have fangs with which to inject venom. Figure 16-1 depicts the characteristics of a nonvenomous snake. 161 Venomous Snakes 376B

Venomous snakes possess venom glands and specialized fangs to inject venom into their prey or as a defense mechanism. It is important to exercise caution and seek immediate medical attention in the event of a venomous snakebite.

It is important to note that the distribution of venomous snakes may vary within states, and some species may be specific to certain regions. When spending time in areas known to have venomous snakes, it is crucial to be aware of the local species, understand their habitats and behavior, and take appropriate precautions to avoid encounters and bites.

Venomous snakes in other parts of the world include sea snakes, the Fer-De-Lance, the Bushmaster, tropical rattlesnake in tropical Central America; the Malayan pit viper in the tropical Far East; the cobra in Africa and Asia; the mamba (or black mamba) in central and southern Africa; and the krait in India and Southeast Asia.

Venomous snakes can be categorized into several groups based on their characteristics and taxonomic classification. The following are some common categories of venomous snakes: • Vipers. • Elapids. • Rear-Fanged Snakes. • Burrowing Asps. • Sea Snakes.

These categories provide a general overview of the different types of venomous snakes based on their taxonomic families and key characteristics. It's important to note that there may be variations within each category, and some venomous snakes may exhibit characteristics from multiple families.

This family of snakes includes some of the most well-known venomous snakes. Vipers are characterized by their large, triangular heads, heat-sensing pits between their eyes and nostrils, and hinged fangs that can fold back when not in use. Examples include rattlesnakes, copperheads, and cottonmouths or water moccasins. See figure 16-2 for characteristics of a venomous pit viper and figure 16-3 on page 163 provides examples of viper snakes. 162 Bites and Stings Copperhead Mojave Rattlesnake Eastern Diamondback Rattlesnake

In the U.S, there are several species of venomous snakes. The following are some of the venomous snakes commonly found in different regions of the country: • Rattlesnakes: Rattlesnakes are a group of venomous snakes known for the rattling sound they produce by shaking their tails. Species such as the eastern and western diamondback, timber and Mojave rattlesnakes are found in various parts of the U.S. • Copperheads: Copperheads are venomous snakes with distinctive copper-colored heads. They are commonly found in the eastern and southeastern regions of the U.S. • Cottonmouths or Water Moccasins: Cottonmouths or Water Moccasins are venomous semi-aquatic snakes primarily found in the southeastern U.S. They are known for their aggressive behavior and are often encountered near bodies of water. • Coral Snakes: Coral snakes are venomous snakes with colorful bands of red, yellow, and black. The Eastern and Texas Coral Snakes are found in specific regions of the southern U.S. • Various Pit Vipers: Pit vipers include venomous snakes that possess heat-sensing pits between their eyes and nostrils. Along with rattlesnakes and copperheads, this category includes species such as the eastern and western Massasauga Rattlesnakes, and the Mojave Desert Sidewinder.

The casualty's condition provides the best information about the seriousness of the situation and how much time has passed since the bite occurred. Pit viper bites are characterized by severe burning pain. Discoloration and swelling around the fang marks usually begins within five to ten minutes after the bite. If only minimal swelling occurs within 30 minutes, the bite will almost certainly have been from a nonvenomous snake or possibly from a venomous snake, which did not inject venom. The venom destroys blood cells, causing a general discoloration of the skin. Blisters and numbness in the affected area follow this reaction. Other signs, which can occur, are weakness, rapid pulse, nausea, shortness of breath, vomiting, and shock.

The venom of viper bites affects the circulatory system and destroys muscle. Severe pain, swelling and change in skin color usually develop within five to 10 minutes and slowly spreads. After several hours, the following signs and symptoms will occur: • Further swelling and changes in skin color. • Bleeding blisters. • Numbness of the affected area.
Other signs and symptoms which may occur include: • Weaknesses. • Rapid pulse. • Nausea. • Vomiting. • Shortness of breath. • Sweating. • Shock. 163

Elapids are a family of venomous snakes known for their fixed front fangs and potent neurotoxic venom. They generally have slender bodies and smooth scales. Famous elapid snakes include cobras, coral snakes, kraits, and mambas. Corals (figure 16-4), cobras (figure 16-5), kraits, and mambas all belong to the same group even though they are found in different parts of the world. All four inject their venom through short, grooved fangs, leaving a characteristic bite pattern. example snake example

To identify a coral snake, a common phrase used in the U.S. is "Red or yellow, kill a fellow; red on black, venom lack." This phrase refers to the color pattern on the snake's bands and serves as a mnemonic device to help distinguish coral snakes from non-venomous snakes with similar markings, such as milk or scarlet kingsnakes. Coral snakes have red bands touching yellow bands, while non-venomous snakes have red bands touching black bands. It's important to remember that this phrase is specific to the U.S. and may not apply to coral snake species found in other regions. When encountering any snake, it is advisable to maintain a safe distance and seek professional assistance if unsure of its venomous nature.

The venom from corals, cobras, kraits, and mambas, which belong to the elapid family, notably affects the central nervous system, producing a distinct set of symptoms that diverge from those caused by pit vipers. Initially, these bites may result in only minimal pain and swelling, leading many individuals to underestimate the severity of the bite. Typically, the onset of neurological symptoms occurs within one to seven hours postbite, including blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, drowsiness, and an increase in salivation and sweating.

If the bite is not addressed quickly with appropriate medical intervention, more severe symptoms can manifest, such as nausea, vomiting, respiratory difficulties, shock, and eventually more critical conditions like paralysis, convulsions, and coma. This progression underscores the necessity of recognizing the potential danger of elapid bites early and seeking immediate medical treatment to mitigate these serious outcomes.

While most rear-fanged snakes are non-venomous, some species within this family possess venomous rear fangs. These fangs are located toward the back of the mouth and are used to subdue their prey. Rearfanged venomous snakes include boomslangs, mangrove, and vine snakes.

Burrowing asps are a family of venomous snakes primarily found in Africa and parts of the Middle East. They have small, fixed front fangs and are adapted for burrowing in sandy or loose soil. Examples include the stiletto snakes and mole vipers.

Sea snakes are a group of venomous snakes that have adapted to life in aquatic environments. They have paddle-shaped tails and can be found in the coastal waters of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Sea snakes have highly potent venom but are generally not aggressive towards humans.

Sea snakes (figure 16-6 on page 165) are found in the warm water areas of the Pacific and Indian Oceans, along the coasts, and at the mouths of some larger rivers. Their venom is VERY venomous, but their fangs are only ¼ inch long. 164 Bites and Stings Venomous Snakebite 42B

Venomous snakes DO NOT always inject venom when they bite or strike a person. However, all snakes may carry tetanus (lockjaw); anyone bitten by a snake, whether venomous or nonvenomous, should immediately seek medical attention.

Venom is injected from the venom sacs through grooved or hollowed fangs. Depending on the species, these fangs are either long or short. Pit vipers have long hollow fangs. These fangs are folded against the roof of the mouth and extend when the snake strikes. This allows them to strike quickly and then withdraw. Cobras, coral snakes, kraits, mambas, and sea snakes have short, grooved fangs. These snakes are less effective in their attempts to bite, since they must chew after striking to inject enough venom (poison) to be effective.

In the event you are bitten, do not attempt to identify and or kill the snake. Freshly killed snakes can continue to bite due to reflexive action. Snake identification is not critical. Medical personnel will treat symptoms by geography and not someone's best guess at a species.

The venoms of different snakes cause different effects. Pit viper venom (hemotoxin [blood toxin]) destroys tissue and blood cells. Cobras, adders, and coral snakes inject powerful venom (neurotoxin [nerve toxin]) which affects the central nervous system, causing respiratory paralysis. Water moccasins and sea snakes have venom that is both hemotoxic and neurotoxic.

In the event of a snakebite, prompt first aid is crucial to minimizing the potential effects of the venom. To perform first aid for a snakebite: • Stay calm and call for medical assistance immediately. Provide medical personnel with information about the snake, if possible, but do not attempt to capture or kill the snake as it may increase the risk of further bites. • Keep the bitten Service member as still and calm as possible. Restrict movement and avoid unnecessary exertion, as it can accelerate the spread of venom in the bloodstream. • Remove any constricting items, such as jewelry or tight clothing, from the affected area, as swelling may occur. • Position the affected limb slightly below the level of the heart, if possible. This can help slow the spread of venom. • Cleanse the wound gently with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Do not apply ice or use a TQ, as they are not effective and can cause additional harm. • Apply a sterile bandage or dress over the bite, ensuring it is snug but not too tight. This can help immobilize the area and reduce the spread of venom. • Encourage the person to remain calm and still, while waiting for medical help to arrive. Monitor their vital signs, such as breathing and heart rate, and be prepared to administer CPR if necessary. 165

The above steps are general guidelines and may vary depending on the snake species and the region. It is crucial to seek medical attention immediately after a snakebite, as they can provide appropriate antivenom treatment and further evaluate the situation.

If accompanying the casualty on CASEVAC to an MTF, observe the casualty carefully for signs and symptoms of an allergic reaction. Continue to monitor the airway, breathing, circulation, vital signs (for first aid purposes; pulse, and respiration), and distal pulse of the bitten extremity, treating for shock, and conserving body heat.

An insect bite or sting can cause great pain, allergic reaction, inflammation, and infection. If not treated correctly, some bites or stings may cause serious illness or even death. When an allergic reaction is not involved, first aid is a simple process. In any case, medical personnel should examine the casualty at the earliest possible time. It is important to identify spiders, bees, or creatures that cause bites or sting, especially in cases of an allergic reaction.

The insects found throughout the world that can produce a bite or sting are too numerous to mention in detail. Commonly encountered stinging or biting insects include the brown recluse spiders, black widow spiders, tarantulas, scorpions, urticating caterpillars, bees, wasps, centipedes, conenose beetles (kissing bugs), ants, and wheel bugs. Upon being reassigned, especially to overseas areas, take the time to become acquainted with the types of insects to avoid.
Arthropods are segmented invertebrates with jointed antennae and legs. They include insects, arachnids, centipedes, and millipedes. See figure 16-7 for examples of venomous arthropods.

Of all deaths due to venomous stings or bites in a year, most are caused by arthropods. Most injuries resulting from venomous arthropods can be prevented by doing the following: • If you are allergic to certain stings or bites, be prepared with the proper medication. • Ask the local inhabitants about the local venomous and harmful arthropods. • Avoid touching unfamiliar arthropods or allowing them to touch you. • Watch where you put your hands and feet. • Before using it, check places where harmful arthropods may hide. ▪ Closets, wall spaces, doorways, and eaves. ▪ Outdoor privies and latrine boxes. 166 Bites and Stings • • • • • ▪ Bed clothing, beds, and sleeping bags. ▪ Shoes, boots, and clothing. ▪ Logs, felled trees, and leaves. ▪ Rocks, boards, and debris. Avoid beehives, ant and wasp nests, and spider webs. Wear foot protection (shoes, boots, and sandals) always. Hang up clothes. Practice good sanitation by removing debris, trash, and board piles. Avoid wearing deodorants, colognes, perfumes, or cosmetics with fragrances.

An insect is a small invertebrate animal characterized by having a segmented body, three pairs of legs, and often one or two pairs of wings. Insects are a diverse group, with over a million known species, and they play important roles in ecosystems as pollinators, decomposers, and prey for other organisms.

First aid treatment for insect bites can vary depending on the type of insect and the individual's reaction. The general first aid steps for treating insect bites are: • Remove the stinger (if applicable): In the case of stinging insects like bees or wasps, it's important to remove the stinger as quickly as possible to prevent further venom injection. Gently scrape it off the skin using a blunt edge like a credit card or your fingernail. Avoid squeezing the venom sac, as it may release more venom. • Wash the bite area: Clean the bite site with mild soap and water to reduce the risk of infection. Be gentle and avoid excessive scrubbing. • Apply a cold compress: To alleviate pain, reduce swelling, and minimize itching, apply a cold compress or an ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the bite area. Do this for 10-15 minutes at a time, several times a day. • Use over-the-counter remedies: Over-the-counter topical creams, ointments, or sprays containing ingredients such as hydrocortisone, calamine lotion, or antihistamines can help relieve itching and inflammation. Follow the instructions and precautions on the product packaging. • Take oral antihistamines: If itching or swelling persists, you can take over-the-counter oral antihistamine to help reduce allergic reactions and relieve symptoms. Consult a pharmacist or health care professional for appropriate dosage and recommendations. • Avoid scratching: Although it may be tempting, refrain from scratching the insect bite to prevent further irritation, infection, or the development of a secondary skin condition. • Monitor for severe re
If the insect type is unknown or if the Service member is experiencing severe or worsening symptoms, it is best to consult a health care professional for proper evaluation and guidance.

An arachnid is a class of joint-legged invertebrate animals that include spiders, scorpions, ticks, and mites. Arachnids are part of the phylum Arthropoda, which also includes insects, crustaceans, and millipedes.

Arachnids are characterized by having two main body segments: the cephalothorax (a fused head and thorax region) and the abdomen. They typically have four pairs of legs attached to the cephalothorax and possess specialized mouthparts called chelicerae, which are used for feeding and defense. Most arachnids also have specialized structures like spinnerets for producing silk (used by spiders for web-building) and a pair of pedipalps that may serve various functions depending on the species.

While spiders are perhaps the most well-known arachnids, other arachnids exhibit unique features. Scorpions have large pincers and a long tail ending in a venomous stinger. Ticks and mites are tiny arachnids that often parasitize animals, including humans, and can transmit diseases. Some arachnids, such as daddy longlegs and sun spiders, have distinct body shapes and behaviors. 167

Arachnids play diverse roles in ecosystems. Spiders, for example, are predators of insects and help control their populations. Arachnids have adapted to various habitats worldwide, from deserts to forests to aquatic environments. Arachnids are a diverse group of invertebrates that exhibit a wide range of adaptations, behaviors, and ecological roles within the animal kingdom.

Among the many species of spiders found around the world, a few are known for their potentially dangerous bites. The most well-known dangerous spider species are the: • Brazilian Wandering Spider. • Sydney Funnel-web Spider. • Black Widow Spider. • Brown Recluse Spider.

The Brazilian Wandering Spider is found in South and Central America and is known for its highly venomous bite. It is considered one of the most venomous spiders in the world. Their venom can cause severe pain, priapism (prolonged erection), and, in rare cases, can be life-threatening.

The Sydney Funnel-web Spider is found in Australia, the Sydney Funnel-web Spider is highly venomous and can be aggressive when threatened. Their venom is potent and can cause severe symptoms, including muscle spasm, difficulty breathing, and in rare cases, it can be fatal. Prompt medical attention is crucial if bitten.

The Black Widow Spider is found in various parts of the world. Females have a distinctive black body with a red hourglass-shaped mark on the abdomen. Their venom contains neurotoxins that can cause intense pain, muscle cramps, nausea, and in severe cases, can affect the nervous system. While bites are rarely fatal, medical attention is still recommended.

The Brown Recluse Spider is found primarily in the U.S. Their bites can cause tissue necrosis (cell death), leading to an ulcerous wound that may require medical attention. Other symptoms can include pain, itching, and systemic effects.

While these spiders are considered dangerous, actual bites and severe reactions are relatively rare. Most spiders are not aggressive and will only bite in self-defense. If bitten by a spider and experiencing severe symptoms, seek immediate medical attention.

Specific risks associated with spider bites can vary depending on a Service member's health, sensitivity, and potential allergies. Therefore, it is always advisable to exercise caution around spiders and seek professional medical advice if a bite occurs.

The most dangerous scorpions are typically found in regions with warm climates, particularly in arid or desert areas. Some locations known for housing dangerous scorpion species are: • North Africa. • Middle East. • Mexico. • Brazil. • India.
Countries in North Africa, such as Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Egypt, are home to highly venomous scorpion species. These species include the Deathstalker scorpion and the Androc tonus australis.

Several countries in the Middle East have venomous scorpions, including Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, and Yemen. The Deathstalker scorpion is found in this region, along with other dangerous species such as the Arabian Fat-tailed scorpion and the Palestine Yellow scorpion.

Mexico is known for its diverse scorpion fauna, and it is home to several highly venomous species. The Bark scorpion is found in various parts of the country, including the notorious Arizona Bark scorpion, which is also found in the southwestern U.S. 168 Bites and Stings
In Brazil, the Brazilian Yellow scorpion is considered one of the most venomous scorpions. It is primarily found in southeastern and southern regions of the country.
India is home to several dangerous scorpion species. The Indian Red scorpion and the Indian Black scorpion are found to live in this region.

While these regions have known populations of dangerous scorpions, encounters with venomous scorpions and severe envenomation are relatively rare. However, it is always advisable to exercise caution and take necessary precautions when in scorpion-prone areas. Figure 16-8 provides an example of a scorpion.

A centipede is a type of arthropod characterized by elongated, multi-segmented creatures with numerous pairs of legs, ranging from tens to hundreds depending on the species. Centipedes are found in various habitats worldwide, including forests, deserts, and tropical regions.

While most centipedes are not considered dangerous to humans, some larger species possess venomous pincers or fangs located on their first pair of legs. When threatened or provoked, they can deliver a painful sting or bite. The severity of the reaction to a centipede sting can vary depending on the species and the individual's sensitivity to the venom. Centipede bites are painful but not life-threatening. If a Service member is stung by a centipede, first aid steps to take are: • Stay calm and move away from the centipede to avoid further stings. • Wash the affected area gently with soap and water to clean the wound and reduce the risk of infection. • Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the sting site. This can help alleviate pain and reduce swelling. • Take over-the-counter pain relievers, such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen, to manage pain if necessary. Follow the instructions and recommended dosage. • Keep the sting site clean and dry and avoid scratching or irritating the area to prevent infection.
If there are signs of an allergic reaction, such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or widespread hives, seek immediate medical attention.

Millipedes, belonging to the class Diplopoda, are arthropods distinguished by their elongated, segmented bodies with two pairs of legs per body segment, excluding the first few segments. These creatures are commonly found in moist environments such as forests, gardens, and areas with decaying vegetation.

Unlike centipedes, millipedes lack venomous pincers or fangs and are generally harmless to humans. However, they possess defensive mechanisms that can release toxins or irritating chemicals, which may cause mild reactions in some individuals, particularly those with sensitive skin.

If a Service member encounters a millipede and experiences irritation or a sting, the recommended first aid steps include: 169 • • • • Washing the affected area gently with soap and water to cleanse the site and remove any secretions from the millipede. Applying a cold compress or an ice pack wrapped in a cloth to reduce swelling and alleviate discomfort at the sting site. Using over-the-counter topical antihistamines or hydrocortisone creams to relieve itching or irritation. Avoiding scratching or further irritating the site to prevent infection.

In cases where there is a severe allergic reaction, characterized by symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or widespread hives, it is crucial to seek immediate medical attention. While millipede stings are typically mild and self-limiting, if symptoms persist, worsen, or if there are concerns about an individual's reaction, consulting a healthcare professional for further advice and treatment is advisable.

Fire ants are a type of stinging ant that are native to South America but have spread to various parts of the world, including the southern U.S, Southeast Asia, and Australia. Fire ants are known for their aggressive behavior and painful stings.

When a fire ant stings, it injects venom into the skin, resulting in a sharp, burning sensation and the formation of a raised, reddish bump. Multiple ants may attack simultaneously, leading to multiple stings. If stung by a fire ant, the first aid steps are to: • Move away from the area where the ants are present to avoid further stings. • Remove any clothing or jewelry that may have ants trapped in them, as they can continue to sting. • Gently wash the affected area with soap and water to clean the site. • Apply a cold compress or ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the sting site. This can help reduce pain and swelling. • Over-the-counter pain relievers, such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen, can be taken to help manage pain if necessary. Follow the instructions and recommended dosage. • Avoid scratching the sting site to prevent infection. If itching is severe, over-the-counter antihistamines or hydrocortisone creams may be used under the guidance of a health care professional. • Monitor the individual for signs of an allergic reaction, such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or widespread hives. If these symptoms occur, seek immediate medical attention.

Fire ant stings can be particularly problematic for individuals who are allergic or hypersensitive to ant venom. In such cases, immediate medical attention should be sought. These first aid steps are general guidelines, and the severity of the reaction may vary from person to person. If there are concerns about the Service member's health or if the symptoms worsen or persist, consult a health care professional for appropriate advice and treatment.

A tick is a small arachnid parasite that feeds on the blood of animals, including humans. Ticks are found in various environments, such as forests, grasslands, and shrubby areas. They latch onto their hosts and can transmit diseases through their bites.

When a tick bites, it burrows its mouth parts into the skin to feed on blood. If you discover a tick attached to your skin, it's important to remove it promptly and take the following first aid steps: • Prepare for tick removal: Use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick as close to the skin's surface as possible. Avoid squeezing or crushing the tick's body. • Remove the tick: Gently and steadily pull the tick upward with even pressure. Do not twist or jerk it. The goal is to remove the entire tick, including its mouthparts. Dispose of the tick by placing it in a sealed bag or container or by submerging it in alcohol. • Clean the bite area: Thoroughly clean the bite area with soap and water or an antiseptic solution to reduce the risk of infection. 170 Bites and Stings • • Apply an antiseptic: After cleaning the bite area, you can apply an antiseptic ointment or cream to further prevent infection. Monitor for symptoms: Keep an eye on the bite site for any signs of an allergic reaction, infection, or the appearance of a rash. If you notice any concerning symptoms, seek medical attention.

Certain tick-borne diseases, such as Lyme disease or Rocky Mountain spotted fever, may take time to manifest symptoms. If in an area where these diseases are prevalent or if you develop symptoms such as fever, rash, joint pain, or flu-like symptoms after a tick bite, it is crucial to consult a health care professional for proper evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment.

Prevention is key when it comes to ticks. To minimize the risk of tick bites, wear protective clothing when in tick-prone areas, use insect repellents containing DEET, perform regular tick checks after outdoor activities, and take appropriate measures to protect pets from ticks as well. DEET (chemical name, N, Ndiethyl-meta-toluamide) is the active ingredient in many repellent products. It is widely used to repel biting pests such as mosquitoes and ticks.

The signs and symptoms of a tick bite can vary depending on factors such as the type of tick, the individual's sensitivity to the tick's saliva, and the presence of any tick-borne diseases. The common signs and symptoms associated with tick bites are: • Redness and swelling: After a tick bite, it is common to experience localized redness and swelling at the site of the bite. This is a normal reaction to the tick's saliva. • Itching or irritation: The bite site may be itchy or irritated, like a mosquito bite. Avoid scratching to reduce the risk of infection. • Tick remnants: If a tick is not promptly and properly removed, parts of the tick's body, such as its mouthparts, may remain embedded in the skin. This can lead to ongoing irritation and a risk of infection. • Rash: In some cases, a small red spot or rash may develop around the tick bite. This can expand over time and may resemble a target-like pattern. It is important to note that not all tick bites result in a rash. • Flu-like symptoms: Tick-borne diseases such as Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, or babesiosis can cause flu-like symptoms. These may include fever, fatigue, headache, muscle aches, joint pain, and swollen lymph nodes. However, these symptoms usually develop days or weeks after the tick bite. • Allergic reaction: In rare cases, individuals may have an allergic reaction to tick bites, resulting in more severe symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swelling, hives, or anaphylaxis. Immediate medical attention is necessary in such cases.

Not all tick bites lead to the transmission of diseases, and most tick bites are harmless. If a Service member experiences any concerning symptoms or if you live in an area where tick-borne diseases are prevalent, seek medical attention for proper evaluation, diagnosis, and appropriate treatment. 171 This page intentionally left blank.

Climatic injuries, also known as weather-related injuries, occur when people's health is negatively affected by extreme weather conditions. These injuries can range from heat-related illnesses to cold-related conditions, and they are often a result of prolonged exposure to harsh environmental elements. Climate plays a significant role in determining the risks individuals face, with hot climates posing dangers of heat exhaustion and heatstroke, while cold climates can lead to frostbite and hypothermia. Understanding the signs, symptoms, and prevention strategies for these climatic injuries is essential in ensuring our well-being and staying safe in different weather conditions.
